articles.title: In Europe, Too, Amazon’s Warehouses Are a Dystopia
articles.author: Li Andersson
articles.content: When you see it, it’s hard to believe that nobody, at any point from planning to installation, raised a hand to say how tone-deaf it was. But there it is, emblazoned in bright colors above the gates where workers enter an Amazon warehouse in Germany: “Work hard. Have fun. Make history.” The corporate Americana and hyperoptimistic bravado are enough to make us wince. In Germany, of all places, words about work above an iron gate also bring to mind a much darker time and another slogan about work and freedom. It’s a terrible look. That gate was our introduction to a fact-finding mission to Amazon warehouses in Germany and Poland. On October 26 and 27, we joined a delegation from the European Parliament’s Committee on Employment and Social Affairs at the company’s sites in Mönchengladbach, Dortmund, and Sosnowiec, near Katowice. The visit was long overdue. In refusing to take part in the European Parliament’s hearings on warehouse working conditions, Amazon showed disrespect for workers’ rights and for democracy. A planned visit fell through in 2023, and the Parliament revoked Amazon lobbyists’ access badges in 2024. This January, the committee finally held a hearing with Amazon representatives and workers. By October, members of Parliament could visit the warehouses without signing nondisclosure agreements and with few restrictions on taking photos or videos. We knew what we were dealing with even before we saw the sign. Amazon workers and their unions have organized campaigns and taken strike action over digital surveillance, punishing work rates, reliance on temp agencies, and the company’s resistance to collective bargaining. Amazon has also been accused of rerouting packages to blunt the impact of strikes. The sign captured much of what we saw and heard during the visit. From the slogans on the walls to the managers’ answers to our questions, we encountered an eerie, over-the-top optimism and a single overriding concern: productivity at any cost. At times, it was nearly impossible to discuss our concerns with the managers who accompanied us. We asked about reports of worker surveillance and algorithmic management, and whether rising productivity targets put workers at greater risk of injury. The managers dismissed our concerns as a misconception. They said they measured workflows, not individual workers. If someone fell behind, then of course it was a manager’s job to help them. Wouldn’t we agree? When we raised collective bargaining, they said they preferred speaking to workers directly. Everyone was earning more than the minimum wage, they told us, and getting good benefits. Wasn’t that a good thing? It felt strange to move through the warehouses with these optimistic, evasive chaperones. At one station, we stopped to watch a worker who was intensely focused and moving very fast. She looked stressed. A manager hurried over to explain that our presence was probably the reason. The next day, at the Polish warehouse, things seemed much calmer. A worker later told us that management had diverted packages away from the site, offered an unpaid day off to anyone who wanted one, and had many of the workers who came in wait in the canteen during our visit. We met with workers and unions in the evenings after our visits. What they told us sounded like it came from a different world from the one the managers had described. The workers described what sounded to us like a digital panopticon . We had been unable to get a clear picture of how Amazon used technology to monitor and discipline workers. The workers had little more insight into what data Amazon collected on them, how it used that data, or how it set their performance targets. But they knew what happened if they fell short. Workers told us that if they went a certain number of minutes without scanning a package, the system counted that time as a break. If they couldn’t keep pace, a manager would keep dropping by their station, smiling, telling them to do better. The uncertainty, combined with constant pressure to go faster, made workers feel paranoid, they told us. If you think you’re always being watched and need to move faster to keep your job or avoid being seen as difficult, you go faster and faster. That is the logic of Jeremy Bentham’s panopticon, which Michel Foucault used to explain how surveillance disciplines people. The threat of punishment gets inside your head and drives you forward. Some workers told us they barely dared to speak to colleagues at the next station, for fear of making them miss a target neither of them could see. Keep your head down and carry on. With even a quick chat out of the question, workers went faster and faster, helping set ever-higher targets they still couldn’t see. Workers and union representatives also told us how Amazon used technology and workplace practices to thwart collective resistance. Union busting and resistance to collective bargaining have been cornerstones of Amazon’s modus operandi in Europe, too. In Italy, the public broadcaster Rai reported that Amazon managers received recordings from people who had infiltrated union meetings during a drivers’ labor dispute. Amazon told Rai it lacked details to comment on the specific allegations and said its TERA team monitors publicly available information for operational risks. In a separate inquiry, Italy’s data protection authority ordered Amazon to stop processing personal data on workers at its Passo Corese site, including information on their health and union activity. This fall, internal documents disclosed in a British Columbia labor dispute described a tool called Atlas that used AI to assess the likelihood of union organizing and other labor activity at Amazon warehouses. The inputs included employee feedback from channels such as Amazon’s Voice of the Associate message board. Amazon told openDemocracy that the tool assessed activity at the site level and that it did not monitor individual workers’ opinions or union affiliations. When we raised the Italian and Canadian reports during our visit, Amazon representatives denied the allegations, with a smile. The workers’ accounts of union busting went beyond technology. In our evening meetings, workers told us the company had deliberately held works council meetings before it had hired all the warehouse workers at some sites, leaving the councils dominated by management and support staff. Workers active in unions said they feared Amazon would find out. They told us they’d seen colleagues passed over for promotions or moved to worse workstations. They said Amazon had hired workers just before a key vote on industrial action at some sites to dilute the vote. Strikers told us they had been met with music blasting from speakers outside the gates. This falls far short of what workers in Europe should expect from employers, even when tensions are running high. We left the warehouses with much the same concern we heard from labor inspectors. Without fuller access to Amazon’s systems, it’s hard to tell exactly how the company uses them to pressure workers. We could see the effects, though. As one worker put it: “It is like modern day slavery, without the whip.” At Amazon, the whip has gone digital, built into an invisible algorithm. It works alongside union busting, making workers think twice before demanding their rights. And it comes with a smile. Our delegation left determined to keep monitoring conditions and supporting Amazon workers. As workers strike and protest this Black Friday in Europe and around the world, the question is how far Europe is willing to go to defend collective bargaining and workers’ right to act together. That means resisting the Americanization of Europe’s labor market and the idea that large employers alone should set pay and working conditions. articles.title: The Glovebox Checklist
articles.author: Britta Hedlund
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Most drivers keep registration papers and a few random receipts in the glovebox, but little for the minutes after a collision. Your phone battery might be low, the other driver may be upset, and important details can be easy to forget when you’re shaken. A small, organized kit can help you contact people, document the scene, and keep essential information together. It won’t prevent a crash, but it can make the aftermath easier to manage. Quick Overview: Keep insurance documents, emergency contacts, a charged phone, basic safety supplies, and an evidence checklist in your car. After a collision, prioritize safety, seek medical care when needed, and record important details promptly. The 10 Essentials to Keep in Your Car You don’t need a bulky emergency kit. A few carefully chosen items can help you stay safe, exchange information, and handle unexpected delays. Keep them organized and check them every few months. 1. Proof of Insurance and Vehicle Registration Keep current proof of insurance and vehicle registration easy to reach. Digital copies can help, but make sure you can access them if your phone loses power or service. Having these documents ready makes exchanging information with another driver or speaking with responding officers easier. 2. A Phone Charger or Power Bank Your phone may be your camera, flashlight, map, and way to contact help. Keep a compatible car charger or charged power bank with the necessary cable. Check the battery periodically so it’s ready when needed, especially if your vehicle’s electrical system is damaged in a collision. 3. Emergency Contacts and a Medical Information Card Keep a printed emergency contact list and a small medical information card in a protected sleeve. Include relevant allergies, medications, and conditions emergency personnel may need to know. Limit sensitive details to what’s useful, and store the card securely in case you cannot communicate clearly after a crash. 4. A Pen and Small Notebook Phones can fail, so keep a pen and notebook handy. Use them to record names, license plates, witness contacts, the location, weather, and any police report number. Write down what happened while your memory is fresh, sticking to observations rather than guesses about who caused the collision. 5. A Flashlight A compact flashlight helps you find documents and see your surroundings after dark. Check its batteries regularly. Using a separate light also preserves your phone battery for calls and photographs. Never step into traffic or approach damaged vehicles in an unsafe position just to get a better look. 6. Reflective Triangles or Roadside Warning Devices Reflective triangles can warn approaching drivers about a stopped vehicle, particularly on busy roads or after dark. Store them securely and learn how to use them beforehand. Only place warning devices when it’s safe; don’t walk into moving traffic or put yourself at risk to set them out. 7. A Basic First-Aid Kit Keep bandages, disposable gloves, gauze, and antiseptic wipes for minor injuries. A first-aid kit is not a substitute for medical care. For serious bleeding, suspected head or neck injuries, or other emergencies, contact emergency services and follow their instructions rather than attempting treatment beyond your training. 8. A Blanket and Bottled Water Waiting for roadside assistance can take longer than expected. A compact blanket helps in cold weather, while bottled water can be useful during a delay in warm conditions. Check stored water periodically and replace it as needed. Depending on the season, consider adding gloves or other practical supplies. 9. A Checklist of Photos to Take Once everyone is safe, use a checklist to document the scene. Photograph each vehicle from several angles, license plates, visible damage, road signs, traffic signals, weather, and relevant debris or skid marks. Don’t delay medical care or put yourself in danger to take pictures. 10. A List of Details to Collect Keep a printed checklist of details to exchange with the other driver and, where relevant, responding officers. Record names, contact details, insurance company and policy information, license plates, vehicle descriptions, witness contacts, and the officer’s name or report number. Insurance matters because not every driver has coverage. The Insurance Information Institute reports that 15.4% of U.S. motorists were uninsured in 2023, according to a 2025 Insurance Research Council study. Its uninsured motorist statistics explain why documenting insurance information and knowing your own coverage can matter. After the Kit Has Done Its Job Once everyone is safe, call 911 if anyone is injured or there’s an immediate hazard. Follow emergency responders’ instructions and request a police report when appropriate. Notify your insurer promptly, describe what you know, and avoid guessing about fault. Seek medical attention if you’re hurt or concerned about possible injuries, even if you initially feel fine. Symptoms of injuries such as whiplash or concussion may appear later. If discomfort develops days after the collision, this guide explains considerations around reporting an injury after a crash. Keep medical records, repair estimates, receipts, photographs, and insurance correspondence together. Organized records make it easier to answer questions later without relying entirely on memory. When a Lawyer Is Worth a Call Legal guidance may be useful when someone is injured, fault is disputed, the other driver appears uninsured, or an insurer requests a recorded statement or proposes a quick settlement before the full impact of the crash is clear. Your notes, photographs, witness details, and insurance information can help an attorney understand the circumstances. For drivers involved in a Chicago-area collision, the car accident attorneys at Chicago Auto Injury Lawyers can provide information about potential next steps. Ten minutes of preparation can make a stressful situation easier to manage. Assemble your kit, check it a few times a year, and replace anything that expires or runs out.

articles.title: Chuck Schumer’s Former Aides Now Lobby for Corporate America
articles.author: Branko Marcetic
articles.content: One of the quirks of Sen. Chuck Schumer’s (D-NY) bid to lead the incoming Democratic Senate majority is that delivering the change voters demanded in November would mean facing off against a small army of his own former staff. Over his many years in Congress, Schumer has seen countless staffers cycle into his office and out into lobbying work for a broad swath of corporate interests: banks, credit card companies, health insurers, drugmakers, cryptocurrency firms, and the AI industry. His former top health advisor lobbies for the American Medical Association, a longtime opponent of single-payer health care. His ex-chief counsel now leads a top lobbying firm’s AI practice as lawmakers weigh how to regulate the industry. Two former financial advisors now lobby for a crypto industry eager to win government-backed legitimacy while keeping the government off its back. Two former legislative directors have lobbied for the private equity industry on housing legislation. A search of federal lobbying disclosures filed since the start of 2025 turns up upwards of a thousand reports naming former Schumer staffers. For his rival for the leadership spot , Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-MD) — like Schumer, a decades-long creature of the DC establishment — the equivalent number is only a fraction of this. The disclosures show a different mix of clients: an airline, a major university, several local airport-related organizations, and a company that develops drones for delivering food and medicine, to name a few. It’s all part of a Washington practice Schumer has excelled at: building a vast network of former staff whose careers he takes an interest in long after they’ve left his office. “People come into Washington in their twenties and thirties, go to the private sector, but stay tethered to their former boss. And the rising tide lifts all boats,” says Jeff Hauser, executive director of the Revolving Door Project. Schumer’s current staff “get extra mentorship from the alumni who are strewn across DC lobbying for various industries,” Hauser says, sometimes simply about benign matters like how to handle their boss. But the resulting close network of loyal former staffers can also be a rich resource in a town that runs on who you know. “These people are super valuable if you’re a corporate interest and looking for who to hire,” he says. This is the fundamental conundrum of Schumer’s potential leadership: if elected majority leader again, the longtime New York senator will have to make good on a historic mandate for change by challenging the very industries that have hired some of his own former senior staff to represent them. Medicare for Few Take, for instance, Matt Fuentes, a partner at the Democratic lobbying firm Avenue Solutions, whose former role as Schumer’s senior health policy adviser for eight years is prominently advertised on the firm’s website. Since 2025, Fuentes has been a lobbyist for the American Medical Association (AMA), a longtime opponent of single-payer health care that has fought national health insurance proposals for more than a century . The AMA has softened its stance in recent years, but its policymaking body voted in 2023 to retain its opposition to single payer . Fuentes doesn’t just lobby for the AMA. His clients include a broad swath of the for-profit health care industry, including some of the large drugmakers Merck, Moderna, Takeda, and Amgen, as well as pharmacy services company HouseRx. His client list also features insurers Blue Cross Blue Shield and UnitedHealth Group (UHG). For the latter, he has lobbied on “prior authorization” — the widely disliked insurer practice of requiring advance approval for care, which can delay treatment and sometimes have deadly consequences. Records show that, for both insurers, Fuentes lobbied on AI and its “correlation to prior authorization and utilization management policies.” UHG and other insurers have long come under fire for the controversial practice of using AI to deny care to and overcharge people, with UHG specifically the subject of a lawsuit alleging it used an algorithm to deny care to older patients. That is one kind of AI use the incoming Congress might seek to regulate. Then there’s Reggie Babin, whose former role in Schumer’s office is prominently displayed on his page on Akin Gump’s website. Babin is co-lead of the firm’s federal AI policy practice. In practice, that means Babin — who worked for five years under Schumer, two of them as his chief counsel from 2020 to 2022 — has lobbied Congress on data centers and AI regulation for several companies, including Microsoft , Adobe , Dropbox , and data center operator STACK Infrastructure . His clients also include OpenAI , the maker of ChatGPT, and the Data Center Coalition, a trade group for data center operators whose board of directors includes executives from across the industry. A 2025 filing lists Babin as lobbying on the coalition’s behalf on “issues related to Section 232 investigations and investment,” a reference to the Trump administration’s trade investigations under Section 232. Tariffs threatened to raise the cost of the AI data center buildout. The concerns about staffers-turned-lobbyists like Fuentes and Babin aren’t theoretical. As the American Prospect reported at the time, a package of antitrust bills aimed at tech giants had broad bipartisan and public support during Joe Biden’s presidency. Schumer, then Senate majority leader, never brought the bills to the floor. “How did the enormous momentum against Big Tech that was developed at the end of the 2010s and built in the early days of the Biden administration fail to lead to significant legislative changes?” says Hauser. “Schumer’s daughters and many former staffers working in Big Tech is a popular explanation.” The New York Post reported at the time that not only were Schumer’s two daughters an Amazon lobbyist and a Facebook product marketing manager, but eighty of his former staffers had gone on to take jobs at those and numerous other tech companies, including Google and Apple. That included Babin, who moved on after the 117th Congress to Akin Gump, which raked in millions of dollars in lobbying fees from tech firms. Sen. Amy Klobuchar, who was championing the legislation, blamed unnamed members of Congress for “giving in to the dominant social media platforms,” while a former Senate staffer told HuffPost that “if Schumer wanted this to happen it would have already happened.” The Prospect reported that Schumer said the votes weren’t there, though he hadn’t conducted a private whip count. Super Intelligence Babin is just one of Schumer’s former senior staff who today lobbies for the AI industry. Another is Lucia Panza, Schumer’s former leadership counsel. She took a position lobbying for Amazon after leaving the Senate and now represents companies before Congress and other federal bodies at Crossroads Strategies. When Panza joined the firm, its CEO noted that “her time advising some of the most influential lawmakers and voices in Washington, D.C.” would be helpful to their clients. During Trump’s second term, her clients have included AI companies and other businesses and trade groups that lobby on AI, such as Motorola and the Advanced Medical Technology Association. One of the AI firms Panza has represented is CoreWeave, a cloud computing firm whose bonds have come under pressure amid concerns about the AI data center buildout on which its business depends. Like Babin, Panza also counts the Data Center Coalition as a client. Records show that Panza began lobbying on the Ratepayer Protection Act for both the coalition and CoreWeave in the third quarter of 2026. The bill would require state regulators and certain utilities to consider standards for recovering grid upgrade costs from large data centers. It passed the House 417–3 in September and met opposition in the Senate . A separate bill addressing data center costs passed the Senate in November , leaving the question of who pays for grid upgrades on the congressional agenda. This is on top of several other Schumer connections knee-deep in the industry. Grace Magaletta, his legislative correspondent from 2019 to 2023, lobbied for Samsung on “artificial intelligence policy issues” as recently as 2025. Josh Vlasto, who worked for Schumer from 2004 to 2010, this election cycle co-headed an AI industry group funding Democratic and Republican super PACs to help elect candidates friendly to the industry. Throughout Trump’s second term, Schumer’s former communications director, Israel “Izzy” Klein — whose firm trumpets his “deep ties to congressional leadership” and who was appointed in October to the Congressional Award’s board of directors by Schumer — has lobbied for Cisco and Larry Ellison’s Oracle. Resolution Public Affairs, whose principals included former Schumer legislative directors Heather McHugh and Meghan Taira, also employed a third former Schumer staffer. The three lobbied for chipmaker TSMC Arizona, a key part of the AI supply chain, and on AI issues for Oracle and the Murdoch family’s News Corp. Maxwell Young, who served several stints in Schumer’s office over the past two decades, including most recently as his senior communications adviser in 2020, has since November 2025 been the head of policy communications for AI giant Anthropic. In September, OpenAI hired Schumer’s daughter away from Amazon to head its lobbying efforts at the state and local levels in the Northeast. Not all of Schumer’s ex-staffers are simply doing the industry’s bidding. Carrie Adams, Schumer’s deputy digital director from January 2017 to June 2018, now lobbies for the AI Policy Network (AIPN). She lobbies Congress and, as of the third quarter of 2026, federal agencies including the State, Treasury, and Commerce Departments on a range of AI issues. AIPN, which has gotten funding from ultrarich AI safety advocates and describes itself as independent, backs more regulation as well as export controls aimed at keeping the United States ahead of China in the AI “race.” Political Currency Former Schumer staffers also work for the cryptocurrency industry as it seeks mainstream legitimacy. One example is Jennifer Brown, a former financial policy adviser to Schumer. After Brown left Schumer’s office in 2025, crypto investment firm Paradigm added her to its Policy Council . In announcing the new members, Paradigm said it wanted to “put the misguided era of anti-crypto policy firmly in the rearview mirror,” just months after the Senate leader — while being advised by her — had failed to extend the tenure of a crypto-skeptical SEC commissioner before Trump was sworn in. Brown joined BGR Group as a lobbyist in January 2025, focusing on financial regulation and tax policy. The firm highlighted her experience under Schumer when it announced her hiring. Many of those issues involve cryptocurrency. Filings list Brown as lobbying for crypto clients including stablecoin issuer Circle, wallet provider Phantom, and crypto-focused investors Dragonfly and Digital Currency Group. Brown also lobbied on crypto regulation in 2025 and 2026 for the Decentralization Research Center, which advocates for keeping cryptocurrency “decentralized” — in other words, free from the control of a single authority, including governments and banks. A Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) memo from September 2025 detailed how members of both the center and BGR (Brown wasn’t listed as an attendee) met with the SEC’s Crypto Task Force to discuss regulation of the crypto industry, and handed them reading materials about decentralization. Brown also lobbied for venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz, headed by billionaire Marc Andreessen, maybe best known as one of the first and most high-profile Silicon Valley oligarchs to shift his allegiance from Democrats to MAGA. Andreessen Horowitz employed Brown to lobby on AI and digital assets. It was one of several of Brown’s clients, like data center operator Galaxy Digital Holdings, that sit at the intersection of crypto and AI. Brown is one of several former senior Schumer staffers who have lobbied for crypto-related clients. That the crypto world will have the possible next Senate majority leader’s allies as its advocates in Congress comes at a pivotal time for the industry, which has sought to shed its reputation for facilitating scams and become a mainstream investment option while remaining as free from government oversight as possible. To get there, the industry has pushed for a Goldilocks-style regulatory regime: just enough to grant it legitimacy and reassure skeptical Americans that buying digital assets is safe, but not enough to seriously step on its toes. But that effort has also aroused concern from experts, who fear the destabilizing effects of having digital assets under a light regulatory touch reshaping the balance sheets of banks and other financial institutions. The collapse of Sam Bankman-Fried’s FTX in 2022 seemed to be a cautionary tale, an episode whose fallout was largely contained within the crypto sector. Under Trump, the industry has moved aggressively to deepen its links to the broader financial system. One former Schumer staffer’s lobbying record illustrates the crypto industry’s push for legitimacy through regulation: Ryan Eagan, the Crypto Council for Innovation’s (CCI) director of US federal affairs, whose nearly decade-long stint advising Schumer on banking policy is the first thing mentioned in his official bio, along with his work with other members of Congress to “advance legislative priorities” like “cryptocurrency policies.” In 2026, Eagan lobbied on a spate of bills for the CCI that illustrate the industry’s “just right” regulatory framework: bills extending established securities and commodities tax rules to digital assets or cracking down on fraud and terrorist financing in the industry, as well as a bill barring the Federal Reserve from issuing a central bank digital currency, a measure criticized for potentially putting a straitjacket on monetary policy in a future economic crisis. One bill, the GENIUS Act, which Trump signed into law in July 2025, requires payment stablecoins to be backed by liquid assets such as dollars or short-term US Treasuries. A 2026 working paper argues that a growing stablecoin market could add to systemic risk by tying stablecoin redemptions to the functioning of the Treasury market. A number of other bills Eagan lobbied on were similarly controversial. The CLARITY Act, along with several other pieces of legislation listed in the lobbying filings involving Eagan, would give the smaller Commodity Futures Trading Commission authority over trading in digital commodities and retain a role for the SEC in regulating securities. The CLARITY Act passed the House in July 2025 with a large bipartisan majority. In September 2026, a Senate vote to advance it failed , 49–50 — but the industry is already planning to run it back in the new, Democratic-led Congress next year, with one expert observing that the midterm result doesn’t mean the bill is dead, but that it simply “changes the authors of the next draft.” Schumer’s fellow New York senator Kirsten Gillibrand, a prominent backer of crypto legislation, has drawn scrutiny for her ties to the industry. The crypto connections do not end there. Filings show that Panza, Schumer’s former leadership counsel, has lobbied on the GENIUS and CLARITY Acts for fintech company Block Inc., credit card trade group Electronic Payments Coalition, and the Financial Services Forum, an industry group representing eight of the largest US financial institutions. (She also lobbied on general crypto issues for Visa and the Securities Industry and Financial Markets Association.) The trio of former Schumer staffers at Resolution Public Affairs likewise lobbied for these two bills for asset manager BlackRock and JPMorgan Chase. Return of Wall Street Meanwhile, several of these same former staffers now also lobby for a financial sector that has long stood in the way of reform in Congress and that many Americans associate with corruption in Washington. The Resolution Public Affairs trio, for instance, lobbied throughout this year for the American Investment Council (AIC), a private equity trade group that fought Joe Biden’s proposed tax hikes in 2021. Among other things, they lobbied on the AIC’s behalf on housing legislation that included limits on purchases of single-family homes by large institutional investors. The federal government enacted those limits in July 2026. The Private Equity Stakeholder Project separately estimates that private equity firms own at least a tenth of US apartments. Besides lobbying for both JPMorgan Chase and Mastercard on the matter of capping credit card rates, they also counted as a client the Investment Company Institute (ICI). They lobbied on a bill the ICI supported that aimed to make it harder to treat nonbank institutions as systemic risks to the economy that need extra regulatory scrutiny. Likewise, Panza has spent Trump’s second term lobbying for a number of finance clients on regulatory issues, including work for Morgan Stanley on the implementation of the Obama-era Dodd-Frank Act. Some also represent the growing gambling industry, which has poured money into politics and lobbying . Jennifer Brown, Schumer’s former banking counsel, has lobbied over the past two years for FanDuel on “federal gaming policy,” while Schumer’s two former legislative directors, Heather McHugh and Meghan Taira, lobbied in 2026 through Resolution Public Affairs for the prediction market platform Kalshi. The reason Taira, who spent a total of eighteen years in Schumer’s office, is no longer at the firm is because in October she cut out the middleman and went to work for Kalshi directly, heading its federal lobbying efforts. It was part of a hiring spree of former Democratic staffers that the company undertook in the lead-up to the GOP’s bloodbath this November. Schumer vs. His Own Staffers It would be easy to say this is simply what happens when you’ve been in Washington for a long time. Schumer’s rival, Van Hollen, has represented Maryland in Congress since 2003, and his former staffers’ lobbying work tells a different story. Some former Van Hollen staffers do represent companies with a stake in the incoming Congress’s agenda. Cassandra Brzezinski, a Van Hollen policy adviser until January 2026, now lobbies for Allstate Insurance, the Financial Technology Association, and the London Stock Exchange Group, the latter on digital assets and AI. John Mitchell, his former legislative aide, lobbied in 2025 for Workday, which sells human resources software that uses AI. Alexander Simpson, a legislative correspondent for Van Hollen when he served in the House, now lobbies for American Airlines. The Van Hollen alumni in the filings generally held less senior positions and represented a different mix of clients. Schumer’s alumni include a former chief counsel and multiple former legislative directors working for some of the biggest companies in health care, finance, and technology. The next Democratic Senate majority leader will have a long to-do list, from expanding Medicare and regulating AI and crypto to lowering housing costs as large financial firms buy up more of the nation’s homes. If Schumer wins back the majority leadership, it may prove the most compelling test yet of just how much influence the Washington revolving door commands. articles.title: Indonesia Luxury Travel
articles.author: Tiqua Jackson
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Once a year, the whole island of Bali goes silent for a day. Nyepi, the Balinese Hindu New Year, shuts the island down completely, airport included, and no hotel concierge can talk anyone onto a plane. A traveller who has paid for a cliff-top villa and a private driver can land on the wrong date and spend the night in a transit lounge somewhere else in Asia. Nyepi is the most dramatic of the planning errors that spoil expensive Indonesian trips, though quieter ones sit alongside it. Almost all can be avoided with a few decisions made early. How far apart are the islands? Few countries are as scattered. Some 6,000 inhabited islands sit among more than 17,000 in total, ringed by over 100,000 km of coastline, and the distance from Aceh at the tip of Sumatra to the far side of Papua is about 5,200 km. The usual first-draft itinerary of Bali and Raja Ampat in a week looks tidy on a screen. In practice it means early check-outs and a lot of time in departure halls. A better shape is two regions, each given room to breathe. Bali paired with Lombok, or Bali paired with the Komodo area of Flores, keeps the connections short. Indonesia luxury tours that plan around domestic flights and private transfers let the whole route run from one confirmed schedule, with each leg timed to the next. With ten days or more, a third region in the east becomes realistic, and Raja Ampat or Sumba then gets the time it deserves. Wet season sunshine is wishful thinking Java and Bali, like most of the country, are driest from April to October. Outside those months, afternoons often bring heavy downpours and boat days are more likely to be cancelled. A week of snorkelling and island-hopping booked for January is a gamble. That doesn't make the wet months a write-off. A slow stay in the hills around Ubud, built on spa treatments and cooking classes, suits the green, damp season well, and rain on a jungle canopy from a covered terrace is no hardship. Trips that depend on calm water and clear skies belong between April and October. Check the Nyepi date first Nyepi follows the Balinese calendar, so it moves each year and usually lands in March. On the day itself, the airport and seaports close, and hotels ask guests to stay on the property, with lights kept low after dark. The fix is simple. Look up the date before booking flights, and keep arrivals and departures well clear of it. Some travellers choose to be there for it. Arriving two days ahead means seeing the ogoh-ogoh parades the evening before, then spending a day of enforced stillness at a resort with nowhere to be. For a honeymoon, that can be the most memorable day of the trip. Look beyond Bali's airport Over half of all foreign tourists land at Bali's Ngurah Rai airport (DPS). That makes sense for a Bali-centred trip. It makes very little sense for one focused on Java or the outer islands, where routing everything back through Denpasar adds flights and nights. Flying into Jakarta and out of Bali, or the reverse, often saves a full day of doubling back. Who is running the trip? A bespoke itinerary across several islands is only as reliable as the people holding it together. Itineraries here shift at short notice: weather can cancel a ferry or close a port, and domestic flights get retimed without warning. Official travel advice recommends large, reputable agents for exactly this reason. Before paying a deposit, ask who rebooks a cancelled connection at night and whether there's a local office on the ground. A small agent found through a social media page may be charming, and may also go quiet when a boat doesn't sail. Is a yacht worth it? For the remote east, often yes. A liveaboard or private phinisi in the Komodo area or Raja Ampat turns long transfers into part of the holiday, with a cook and a crew that knows the anchorages. Arriving by private yacht is also more straightforward than many assume. A visit permit valid for 30 days needs only three days' notice, and it can be renewed once for another 30. For those who prefer a larger ship, cruises call at Benoa in Bali and Makassar in Sulawesi, among other ports. Leave room for the villa It's easy to pay for an infinity pool and never sit by it. Two nights per stop sounds efficient until each stay becomes a check-in and a packing session with a dinner squeezed between. Three or four nights at each place gives time for slow mornings and the afternoon nobody planned. Lazy days are the point of a high-end trip, and they need gaps in the schedule. Visas and clocks For most short trips, a visa on arrival or an e-visa is enough. It's valid for 30 days and can be extended once for another 30. Anyone staying longer than a month should arrange the extension before the first period runs out, and a reputable operator can usually help with the paperwork. Indonesia also spans three time zones, from UTC+7 in Java to UTC+9 in Papua, with Bali and Lombok on UTC+8. There's no daylight saving time. A flight from Bali to Jakarta lands an hour "earlier" on the clock, which matters when a private transfer is waiting. Booking confirmations should always show local time. Where to start First, pick the travel month and check it against the Nyepi date and the dry season. Second, choose two regions and the entry and exit airports that suit them, adding a yacht leg if the eastern islands are on the list. Third, shortlist an established operator and ask how they handle changes. Confirm visa length and time zones before the flights are ticketed.

articles.author: Sejal Desai
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Medical costs can arise unexpectedly, making adequate health coverage essential for managing expenses during hospitalisation, treatment or serious illnesses. However, with several coverage options and policy features available, selecting a suitable plan can be confusing. Understanding the key factors to compare can help families choose coverage that matches their healthcare needs and budget. Keep reading to understand the top 5 health insurance plans for families and the key factors you should check before selecting one. What Are the Top 5 Health Insurance Plans for Families? Different families have different healthcare requirements. A young family may benefit from a family floater, while a family with elderly parents may need separate senior citizen coverage. The following are five common health insurance options that families can consider: Family Floater Health Insurance Plan A family floater plan covers multiple family members under one policy with a shared sum insured. For example, a ₹10 lakh family floater provides a total coverage of ₹10 lakh that can be used by any insured family member during the policy year. This type of policy can be a convenient and cost-effective option for young families, particularly when members have relatively similar healthcare needs. What should you check? Total sum insured available for the entire family Maximum number of members allowed Eligibility of children and parents Waiting periods for pre-existing diseases Sum insured restoration benefits Network hospital availability One important point to remember is that the sum insured is shared. Therefore, a large claim by one member can reduce the amount available to other family members during the same policy year. Individual Health Insurance Plans An individual health insurance plan provides separate coverage for each insured person. For example, if four family members each have an individual policy of ₹5 lakh, each person has their own ₹5 lakh sum insured. This can be useful when family members have significantly different ages or healthcare requirements. What should you check? Individual sum insured Premium for each member Coverage for pre-existing conditions Room rent and other applicable limits Waiting periods Cashless hospitalisation facilities Although individual policies can cost more than a family floater, they prevent one person's claim from reducing another family member's available coverage. Senior Citizen Health Insurance Plan Families with parents or other members aged 60 years and above may consider separate health insurance for parents. These plans are designed around healthcare requirements that can become more significant with age. Separate coverage can also prevent older members from increasing the premium of a family floater intended for younger family members. What should you check? Entry age and renewal terms Coverage for pre-existing diseases Disease-specific waiting periods Comparing health insurance plans on a consistent set of criteria—rather than selecting based on premium alone—tends to surface meaningful differences in what each plan actually covers for the conditions most likely to arise. Co-payment requirements Hospitalisation coverage Cashless hospital network Sub-limits, if applicable Pay particular attention to co-payment clauses, as they can require the insured to pay a specified portion of an eligible claim. Critical Illness Insurance Plan Critical illness insurance provides a fixed payout when the insured is diagnosed with a covered critical illness, subject to the policy terms. Conditions covered can include illnesses such as cancer, heart attack, stroke and kidney failure, depending on the policy. Unlike regular health insurance, which generally covers eligible medical expenses, critical illness insurance typically provides a lump-sum benefit after a covered diagnosis. What should you check? Critical illnesses covered Definition of each covered illness Waiting period Survival period, if applicable Payout amount Exclusions and policy conditions This cover can work as a supplement to regular health insurance, particularly for families concerned about the financial impact of a serious illness. Top-Up and Super Top-Up Health Insurance Plans Top-up and super top-up plans can increase a family's overall health insurance protection without requiring a similarly large increase in the base policy's sum insured. A top-up generally applies when an individual claim crosses the specified deductible, while a super top-up generally considers eligible medical expenses cumulatively during the policy period. The exact terms vary by policy. For example, a family with a ₹5 lakh base policy may consider additional coverage to protect against larger medical expenses. What should you check? Deductible amount Whether the deductible applies per claim or cumulatively Total additional coverage Coverage exclusions Whether the policy works alongside your existing health insurance Renewal conditions These plans can be useful when families want to increase their financial protection against high medical expenses. Factors to Consider in Health Insurance for Family A family health insurance plan that lets all members share a single pool of cover is worth comparing directly against individual plans to see which distributes risk more cost-effectively given the family's age spread and health profile. Before selecting a family health insurance policy, keep in mind the following points to have proper coverage and financial security: Plan and Sum Assured: Determine whether you need a family floater policy or should opt for separate health insurance for parents. Coverage and Benefits: Verify coverage for hospitalisation, OPD, home care, modern treatments, and expenses incurred before and after hospitalisation. Waiting Period: Compare waiting periods for pre-existing diseases and specific treatments. Co-payment and Sub-limits: It is always wise to choose plans that do not have any co-payments and sub-limits in order to save your money. Exclusions and Add-ons: Review exclusions and consider useful add-ons such as critical illness cover. Insurer and Claim Service: Check the insurer's claim settlement record, hospital network and customer service before purchasing. Check the PED Waiting Period: A shorter waiting period for pre-existing diseases can allow you to become eligible for related claims sooner, subject to the policy terms. The key is to compare the policy features, not just the premium. Keeping Track of What Each Member Needs A family health plan purchased when only one member had a pre-existing condition may need a review once a second member's health status changes. Many family floaters allow additions to the policy, but the premium recalculation and any new waiting periods depend on the insurer's specific terms, which are worth checking before an addition becomes urgent. Choosing among the top 5 health insurance plans for family requires comparing coverage, premiums, waiting periods, exclusions and benefits. A family floater may suit younger families, while separate policies or additional covers can provide better protection for elderly members and those with higher health risks.

articles.title: Slow Vendor Setup
articles.author: Britta Hedlund
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. When a small business wins a contract with a large organization, it often feels like the hard part is over. The proposal was accepted, the price agreed and the work scheduled. Then comes a stage few owners plan for: getting set up as an approved vendor so they can actually be paid. For many small suppliers, that step brings weeks of forms, emails and follow-ups before a first invoice can be processed. For a company with a big cash cushion, the delay is a nuisance. For a small business with payroll due every two weeks, it can be a real strain. How large organizations handle supplier setup has a quiet but direct effect on the smaller firms, and the workers, that depend on them. What Supplier Setup Involves Before a large buyer can pay a new supplier, it needs to collect and confirm several pieces of information. These usually include: Contact details for the business and its billing team. Banking information for receiving payments. Legal identity checks to confirm the company is genuine. Compliance screening, such as checks against sanctions lists. Tax forms and certifications, plus insurance documents where required. Agreed payment terms, so both sides know when invoices are due. Once everything is approved, the supplier's record is created in the buyer's finance system. Only then can invoices move through and payments go out. Where The Process Breaks Down In many organizations, this work still runs through email chains and spreadsheets. A supplier sends documents in whatever format it has. Someone on the buyer's side copies the details into the finance system by hand. Questions go back and forth between procurement, accounts payable and the supplier, often with long gaps between replies. Each handoff creates room for error. A single wrong digit in a bank account number can send a payment to the wrong place. Duplicate supplier records can cause confusion over which details are current. When something goes wrong, there's often no clear record showing where the mistake happened, so fixing it takes even longer. Large organizations feel these problems as extra workload. Accounts payable teams spend a meaningful share of their time answering supplier questions, and many of those questions trace back to setup errors. Small suppliers feel the same problems as missing money. Why Delays Matter More For Small Firms A large corporation can absorb a late payment without much disruption. A small contractor, caterer, cleaning company or local manufacturer often can't. Many small businesses operate on thin margins and pay their staff before their own customers pay them. When a first payment slips by several weeks, owners may dip into savings, delay their own pay, lean on credit or hold off on hiring. A misdirected payment makes things worse. Recovering money sent to the wrong account can take days or weeks, depending on the banks involved. During that time, the supplier has done the work, the buyer believes it has paid, and the people who did the work are still waiting. The Fraud Risk For Everyone Supplier setup is also one of the most common entry points for payment fraud. Criminals often impersonate real vendors and send convincing emails asking a buyer to update bank details. If those changes aren't verified, the next legitimate payment lands in the fraudster's account. Both sides lose. The buyer may have to pay twice or absorb the loss. The real supplier waits even longer for money it has already earned, sometimes while the two companies sort out who's responsible. Unverified banking information is one of the clearest weak points in the entire process of buying and paying for goods and services. How Digital Tools Change The Picture Supplier onboarding software replaces much of the manual back-and-forth with a structured, self-service process. Instead of emailing documents, a new vendor registers through a secure portal, enters its own contact and banking details and uploads the required paperwork. The system checks the data as it's entered, runs compliance screening automatically and routes the registration to the right people for approval. Once approved, verified details flow into the buyer's finance system without being retyped. The same approach applies when details change. Suppliers can update their own banking or address information, but those updates go through the same verification and approval steps as the original registration. That makes it much harder for a fraudulent request to slip through. For suppliers, the practical benefits are fewer emailed requests, faster setup and quicker access to first payment. Many portals also let vendors submit invoices and check payment status themselves, rather than calling or emailing to ask where their money is. Setup that once took weeks can often be finished within hours to a few business days. What Buyers Can Do Organizations that work with many small suppliers can take several steps to make the process fairer and faster: Give new vendors one clear channel for registration. Ask only for the information each type of supplier actually needs. Verify every bank detail change through a trusted contact. Track how long setup takes from contract to first payment. Let suppliers check invoice and payment status on their own. Measuring the time from contract signature to first payment is especially revealing. Many organizations have never looked at that number, and it often shows where delays build up. What Small Suppliers Can Do Small businesses can protect themselves too. Keeping tax forms, insurance certificates and banking letters ready in digital form speeds up registration with any new customer. Asking early about payment terms and setup requirements avoids surprises. Owners should also treat any request to change bank details with caution, whether it comes to them or is made in their name, and confirm such requests by phone with a known contact. A Shared Interest In Getting It Right Supplier setup can seem like routine administrative work, but it shapes how quickly small businesses get paid and how safely money moves between organizations. When the process is slow and error-prone, smaller firms and their employees often bear the cost. When it's clear, verified and largely self-service, buyers reduce their own workload and risk, and suppliers get paid for their work on time. That outcome serves both sides of every contract.

articles.title: Professional Book Publishing
articles.author: Tiqua Jackson
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Finishing a manuscript is an important milestone, but getting a book into readers’ hands requires more than writing. Editing, cover design, formatting, distribution, and promotion all influence how a book is presented and discovered. Choosing the right publishing support can help authors make informed decisions and avoid common challenges during publication. For many independent writers, publishing also creates opportunities to share personal experiences, cultural perspectives, and stories that might not find space through traditional publishing channels. However, limited budgets, technical requirements, and unfamiliar publishing procedures can make the process difficult, particularly for first-time authors. Today, writers can choose between independent publishing platforms and companies offering professional book publishing assistance. Some platforms allow authors to upload and distribute books independently, while others provide editing, printing, design, and book marketing services. The right approach depends on the author’s experience, budget, and publishing objectives. For writers comparing book publishing companies, understanding these differences is essential. Amazon Kindle Direct Publishing, Barnes & Noble Press, Lulu, USA Book Publishing Services, BookBaby, and IngramSpark offer distinct approaches to getting books published. Exploring their services can help authors identify which options align with their publishing goals. Amazon Kindle Direct Publishing (KDP) Amazon Kindle Direct Publishing (KDP) is a self-publishing platform that allows authors to publish books directly through Amazon’s marketplace. Its publishing tools are made especially for independent writers who want to manage their work without securing a traditional publishing contract. The platform supports Kindle eBooks, paperbacks, and hardcovers. Printed editions use print-on-demand technology, meaning books are manufactured when customers place orders. This eliminates the need for authors to purchase large quantities of inventory before publication. KDP’s self-publishing services allow writers to upload manuscripts, submit cover files, choose book categories, establish prices, and monitor sales. Formatting resources and preview tools help authors prepare digital and printed editions according to Amazon’s publication requirements. Authors generally retain control over their work, although optional programs such as KDP Select involve specific eBook exclusivity conditions. KDP also provides access to Amazon’s established customer marketplace, where readers can discover and purchase independently published titles. However, KDP primarily supplies a platform for publishing rather than complete editorial assistance. Writers are responsible for manuscript quality, design, and promotion, making the service particularly relevant to authors comfortable handling production independently. Barnes & Noble Press Barnes & Noble Press is the self-publishing platform operated by American bookseller Barnes & Noble. It provides independent writers with opportunities to publish digital and printed books through an established retail ecosystem. The platform supports eBook publishing alongside paperback and hardcover printing. Authors can upload publication-ready manuscripts, provide book descriptions, set prices, and prepare their titles for sale through Barnes & Noble’s online bookstore. Digital editions can also reach readers using NOOK devices and applications. Its self-publishing services include publishing tools, formatting guidance, print-on-demand options, and sales reporting. Authors can also order printed copies for personal use, allowing them to review their books or obtain physical editions for events. Barnes & Noble Press provides educational resources and promotional guidance, although publishing online does not automatically secure placement in physical bookstores. For authors seeking additional retail exposure, the platform offers a way to reach Barnes & Noble customers while maintaining responsibility for manuscript preparation and most marketing activities. It can also complement other publishing channels when distribution agreements permit. Lulu - Publishing and Print on Demand Solutions Lulu offers publishing and printing services to authors, educators, businesses, and independent publishers. Its functions include flexible book production, allowing customers to print individual copies or larger quantities according to their requirements. Print-on-demand technology is central to Lulu’s approach. Instead of investing in substantial inventory, authors can have books printed after orders are received. This makes smaller publishing projects and specialised publications more manageable. Lulu supports paperback, hardcover, coil-bound, and saddle-stitched formats. Writers can also select different paper types, trim sizes, and printing specifications, depending on their projects. These options are useful for novels, children’s books, workbooks, photography collections, and educational materials. Its book publishing services include publishing tools, formatting resources, eBook options, and retail distribution for eligible titles. Through Lulu’s Global Distribution program, qualifying books can become available through participating online retailers. Lulu Direct additionally supports selling printed books through an author’s own ecommerce website. Lulu provides production and distribution infrastructure rather than personalised manuscript development. Authors seeking professional editing or specialised cover design may need to arrange those services separately. USA Book Publishing Services USA Book Publishing Services is an independent self-publishing and creative services provider supporting authors throughout different stages of book development, production, and promotion. Unlike platforms focused primarily on uploading finished manuscripts, the company offers professional assistance with tasks that writers may not have the expertise or resources to manage independently. Book Publishing Services Preparing a manuscript for publication involves technical requirements that extend beyond the writing process. USA Book Publishing Services assists with manuscript preparation, formatting, and publication coordination, helping authors develop their work for digital and printed formats. This form of professional book publishing assistance can be useful for writers unfamiliar with file preparation, interior layouts, and production specifications. Self Publishing Services The company’s self publishing services assist authors pursuing independent publication while getting help with formatting, production, and related requirements. This approach allows writers to remain involved in publishing decisions without managing every technical detail themselves. Authors should nevertheless review individual contracts to understand ownership, distribution arrangements, and included services. Editing and Proofreading Editorial refinement is another component of the company’s services. USA Book Publishing Services provides editing and proofreading assistance intended to improve manuscript clarity, language accuracy, and readability. Developmental editing focuses on overall content and structure, while line editing and copyediting address expression, consistency, and grammatical accuracy. Proofreading helps identify remaining errors before publication. Cover Design and Illustration A book’s appearance can influence how readers interpret its genre, subject, and tone. USA Book Publishing Services offers book cover design and illustration assistance, supporting authors who require professional visual presentation. Design considerations include typography, imagery, composition, and compatibility with print and digital formats. Illustration services are also relevant to children’s books and publications requiring original artwork. Book Marketing Services USA Book Publishing Services also provides book marketing services aimed at improving visibility and supporting audience engagement. Its promotional offerings include author branding, social media activities, advertising, and outreach-related assistance. Effective promotion requires identifying potential readers and choosing suitable communication channels. These services can help authors plan promotional activities before or after publication, although marketing outcomes depend on several factors beyond service delivery. Author Support Beyond individual production tasks, the company provides book publishing support for complex publication requirements by coordinating different project stages. This assistance may be particularly relevant to writers unfamiliar with formatting standards, publishing procedures, or promotional planning. Authors considering its services should evaluate project costs, contractual terms, deliverables, and the level of guidance included. BookBaby BookBaby provides publishing and production services for independent authors seeking assistance with manuscript preparation, design, printing, and distribution. Its model combines professional services with publishing platforms, allowing writers to obtain support at different stages of production. BookBaby’s book publishing services include editing, proofreading, cover design, interior formatting, and eBook conversion. Authors can select individual services or explore packages combining several publishing requirements. The company also offers paperback and hardcover printing, print-on-demand options, and digital distribution. Its eBook distribution network connects authors with retailers such as Amazon, Apple Books, Kobo, and Barnes & Noble. BookBaby provides book marketing services covering promotional planning, advertising-related assistance, and tools needed to support reader awareness. Its publishing specialists also help authors understand available production options. For writers who prefer coordinated assistance rather than managing multiple independent contractors, BookBaby presents a service-based alternative to uploading publication-ready files directly to a platform. Authors should compare package costs, distribution terms, and promotional deliverables before selecting services. IngramSpark IngramSpark focuses on print production and distribution for independent authors and small publishers. Operated within Ingram’s publishing infrastructure, the platform helps writers make their books available through a broad network of booksellers and retailers. Its self-publishing services support paperback, hardcover, and eBook publication. Print-on-demand allows physical copies to be manufactured as orders arrive, reducing the need to maintain large amounts of inventory. IngramSpark’s distribution network connects eligible publications with bookstores, libraries, online retailers, and international markets. However, availability through a distribution catalogue does not guarantee that a particular bookstore will stock a title. The platform also provides publishing resources, guidelines, pricing tools, and a book-building tool. It does not currently offer conventional manuscript editing, custom typesetting, or custom cover design as direct services. For authors who already have publication ready materials, IngramSpark offers an opportunity to explore wider distribution. Its primary contribution is publishing rather than complete editorial or promotional assistance. What Should Authors Consider When Choosing a Publishing Partner? Selecting suitable book publishing support starts with identifying which services a manuscript requires. Authors with finished, professionally edited books may only need printing and distribution, while first time writers could benefit from editing, design, formatting, and publication guidance. Costs also vary between providers. Some self-publishing services allow authors to upload books without upfront charges, although printing costs and retailer deductions may apply. Service based providers may charge for editing, design, production, and marketing packages. Distribution opportunities deserve careful evaluation. Authors should understand where their books will be available, which formats are supported, and whether additional fees or restrictions apply. Marketing is another consideration. Professional book marketing services may include advertising, publicity, social media campaigns, or audience research, but promotional activity does not guarantee commercial success. Clear deliverables and realistic expectations are important. Finally, writers should examine copyright ownership, ISBN arrangements, royalty calculations, publishing control, and contract termination terms. Comparing these details helps authors distinguish between book publishing companies and select services that fit their individual requirements. Final Thoughts on Finding the Right Publishing Support The publishing market offers several routes for authors with different needs. Amazon KDP and Barnes & Noble Press provide direct publishing platforms, while Lulu and IngramSpark focus on printing and distribution infrastructure. USA Book Publishing Services and BookBaby offer broader book publishing services, including editorial preparation, design, production, and promotional assistance. Each option serves a different purpose within the independent publishing industry. Ultimately, choosing the right book publishing support depends on an author’s budget, preferences, distribution objectives, and desired level of professional involvement. Reviewing services carefully and understanding contractual responsibilities can help writers make informed decisions before publication.
