articles.title: In Spain, the Indignados’ Parties Are Dwindling Fast
articles.author: Carlos Delclós
articles.content: On September 23, Maricarmen Abascal was carried on a stretcher out of her apartment in the Retiro district of Madrid, where she’d been living since 1956. She was eighty-seven, disabled, and had limited mobility. Neighbors and members of the Madrid Tenants’ Union had formed a human chain to stop the eviction. This time, the police broke through it. As she was carried out, the crowd shouted that she was not alone. Two weeks later, she died in a hospital, before she could return to her home, under an agreement with her corporate landlords that arrived far too late. Her case set off a massive wave of mobilization led by a confederation of tenants’ unions. On September 26, marches under the slogan “Not One More Maricarmen” filled the streets of some forty towns and cities. In Madrid, protesters pitched hundreds of tents in the iconic Puerta del Sol, the public square that the anti-austerity Indignados occupied in 2011, and encampments soon spread across Spain. But on October 2, after Pedro Sánchez’s center-left government proposed two emergency housing decrees, the conservative Partido Popular, the far-right Vox, and the right-wing Catalan-nationalist Junts joined forces to block the measures. Sánchez, who represents the Partido Socialista Obrero Español (PSOE), responded by calling snap elections for November 29, this Sunday. With parliament dissolved, its standing committee revived the main decree by a single vote, extending the ban on evicting vulnerable households through 2030. Pressure has been building in Spain’s housing system for two decades. In 2006, at the height of a speculative bubble, the V de Vivienda (“V for Housing”) movement summed up a generation’s prospects in its blunt slogan: “You’re not going to have a house your whole f — ing life.” After the bubble burst in 2008, dragging the economy down with it, some of its more prominent activists founded the Mortgage Victims’ Platform (PAH), which became a pillar of the broader Indignados Movement. Today rents are at record highs, and housing has become a primary driver of inequality in Spain. According to the Spanish Youth Council , only 14.5 percent of Spaniards ages sixteen to twenty-nine lived away from their parents last year, the lowest share on record. But the cracks run deeper than young tenants’ case alone. Bank of Spain data show that the share of households headed by sixty-five- to seventy-four-year-olds owning additional real estate properties nearly doubled, to 62 percent, while homeownership among those thirty-five to forty-four fell dramatically. Increasingly, Spain’s class structure is dividing along the lines of rentiers and lifelong tenants, with inheritances largely deciding who ends up where. The right-wing opposition criticizes the Left’s policy focus on rent control, noting that the supply of long-term rentals collapsed in Catalonia after price caps took effect in 2024. But much of that housing moved into temporary contracts, which the 2023 Housing Law left unregulated despite warnings from tenant unions and the PSOE’s left-wing coalition partners. Seasonal contracts in Catalonia rose 45 percent over the caps’ first year. The Socialists now back closing the loophole in the national legislation. Sympathy for the evicted reaches well beyond the Left. In an early October survey by Spain’s state-run Center for Sociological Research (CIS), housing topped the list of national problems even among right-wing voters. Two-thirds of Partido Popular and Vox voters agreed that housing should be seen as a right rather than a commodity. Yet their parties had just voted down the decrees. For now, the polls are unkind to the governing broad-left coalition. Most show the Partido Popular and Vox on course for a majority coalition. Hostility toward Sánchez is especially strong, bolstered by the corruption conviction of his former right-hand man, José Luis Ábalos, amnesty for Catalan separatist leaders, and July’s mass crossing of people into Spain’s North African enclave of Ceuta, among other issues. The Spanish Exception This prognosis is especially striking since, for much of the past decade, Spain has stood out as a relatively progressive exception in European politics. After years of contentious mobilization, the energy of the Indignados’ anti-austerity protests was eventually channeled into government. Since 2018, Sánchez’s governments — supported by Podemos from the outside, before the Socialists and Podemos formed a coalition in 2020 — have raised the minimum wage by more than 60 percent, curbed temporary labor contracts, and opened a path to legal status for undocumented migrants. GDP growth has also outpaced most of the eurozone. Abroad Sánchez recognized a Palestinian state, imposed an arms embargo on Israel, and refused NATO’s new spending target, becoming a standard-bearer for left-wingers internationally. At home, however, he is seen as a polarizing figure. Many observers read today’s situation as the end of an era. But in 2023, most polls similarly predicted a right-wing majority that didn’t materialize on Election Day, and even now a large share of voters remain undecided. What does seem to be ending is the political cycle that began in the squares in 2011 and entered parliament in 2015. Fragmented and consumed by personal hostilities, the Left’s most familiar faces will compete against one another on November 29. Sumar, the coalition led by Deputy Premier Yolanda Díaz, won thirty-one seats in 2023. Podemos left the coalition early in the new term, citing its exclusion from the cabinet and its inability to operate inside Sumar’s parliamentary group. Sumar’s successor, the Frente Amplio, led by former Barcelona Mayor Ada Colau, herself a founder of the PAH, is now competing against Podemos. The latter, in turn, has allied with regional parties in several provinces, most notably the pro-independence Esquerra Republicana in Catalonia. Tellingly, the dispute began over process. Podemos insisted on an open vote to choose candidates while Frente Amplio demanded a prior political agreement on the lists. That two parties born of a movement for “real democracy” could not agree on how to make a democratic decision is the clearest symptom of a deeper failure, namely, a lack of proper mechanisms for deliberation between the coalition’s different currents. At its founding assembly in 2014, Podemos opted for a centralized structure designed to win elections quickly; the local circles that had given birth to it soon lost their influence. Internal democracy came to mean online votes, which some members criticized as simply ratifying decisions already made at the top. Without shared rules for settling disagreements, conflicts ended in splits: Íñigo Errejón’s departure in 2019, Podemos’s break with Sumar in 2023, and now this one. Sumar, for its part, was built around Díaz, with its internal structures assembled ad hoc only later. What filled the vacuum was personality. Podemos was born at a peculiar moment in Spain’s media landscape, when political talk shows were booming on television and social media was beginning to set their agenda. Pablo Iglesias, a political scientist who had honed his style on a small online TV show, became a fixture of prime-time debates, and in 2014 the party put his face on the ballot. Few parties have exploited the personalization of politics so skillfully, or at such an opportune time. But a party organized around the visibility of its leaders has no way to resolve their conflicts other than a politics of personal brands, neglecting development of the internal mechanisms needed for movements to outlive their leaders. New Generation Yet even amid the apparent demise of these party vehicles, a new political generation is emerging: people who came of age after the 2008 crash, organized in tenant unions rather than parties, but also far less hesitant than the Indignados to situate themselves ideologically. The question that will shape Spain’s next decade is not only who governs but who participates in politics, and how. For the Indignados, participation was not just turnout but a broad set of radical democratic practices: assemblies in the squares, consensus-based decision-making, self-management, and civil disobedience. As they grew into their institutional roles, the parties that grew out of the squares left these practices behind. The movements did not abandon such principles, but they have also changed. While the Indignados resisted ideological labels in their condemnation of the entire political class, today’s housing movement is explicitly left-wing. Part of it, most notably the fast-growing Movimiento Socialista, openly contests the PSOE’s claim to the word “socialism.” Meanwhile, they do not reject electoral strategy as aggressively as the movement did in 2011. Tellingly, an essay in one of its main outlets rejected abstention from voting as “antipolitics” and argued for a third position independent of both the (pro-government) progressive and reactionary blocs. If the Sánchez era is to end, its author Axel Altadill claimed, it should be brought down later by a working-class movement, not now by the reactionary right. This position, and the issue of housing rights, is all the more relevant given recent research on political polarization. A study of forty-one elections in twenty countries, including Spain, by political scientists Mariano Torcal and Paul Beck finds that conversations across party lines rarely soften partisan hostility, and that polarized citizens tend to avoid them altogether. In the October CIS survey, about four in ten Partido Popular and Vox voters backed restricting home purchases by speculative investors, and as many or more wanted tighter rules on seasonal rentals. Over 40 percent of lower-income right-wing voters support banning evictions of vulnerable households. Yet only 9 percent of Partido Popular voters and 7 percent of Vox voters rated the government’s decrees on this issue favorably. It seems the more a policy is identified with Sánchez, the less its content matters to conservative voters. In contrast, housing rights cut across party lines when they emerge as a bottom-up demand. Tenant organizing seeks to bridge the divides electoral spectacle tends to amplify. On November 11, Spain got a taste of what bottom-up organizing can achieve: its first general strike in fourteen years, a nationwide stoppage in which workers across sectors walked off the job for a day. It began as a demand from tenant unions, was taken up by the country’s main labor federations, and culminated in marches that drew millions into the streets. In practically all of Spain’s major cities, tenant unions led the marches, with the leaders of the largest labor unions gathering behind their banners. As Valeria Racu, a spokesperson for the Madrid Tenants’ Union, put it: “Whoever governs, we will not tolerate another four years without tackling this country’s biggest problem.” In this context, Spain’s still-undecided voters will play a key role this Sunday. According to the CIS data from October, they make up about one-sixth of the electorate, and those among them who voted in the last general election in 2023 largely backed the Left over the Right. Half of these potential voters support at least eight of the eleven measures in October’s government housing decrees, but only 17 percent claim to trust Sánchez. So, while undecided voters want a comprehensive housing agenda, they don’t seem to trust anyone to see it through. This pattern is most pronounced among the one-fifth of all undecided voters who are under thirty-five years of age. A massive 94 percent of this group say housing should be a right rather than a market good, yet only about half rate the Sánchez government’s housing decrees favorably. This new political generation has yet to find an electoral vehicle. The energy with which it comes to the ballot box may decide whether Sánchez’s coalition remains in office or whether the far right enters government. But whoever wins the elections will face a society with tenants organized in cities throughout Spain and unions newly willing to strike. Maricarmen’s neighbors were unable to save her home, but their promise echoes beyond her doorstep. It is becoming a mass movement with its own political program, ready to confront whoever governs Spain after this Sunday’s vote. articles.title: Van Hollen as Majority Leader
articles.author: Richard W. Behan
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Big shoutout for the blue tsunami. Sooner than we dared dream MAGA is dangling from the ropes. When the Democratic Congress convenes next January we can reasonably expect reversals of Trump’s most heinous policies: the Iran war, the tariffs, the drastic cuts in healthcare and nutrition benefits. Jeffries in the House, and both Schumer and Van Hollen in the Senate seem willing and able to advance this agenda; all three have verbalized most of it. Reclaiming a pre-Trump status quo seems a Congressional shoo-in, and if Trump vetos the reform measures he’ll be orchestrating a total collapse of the Republican Party in 2028. MAGA will be a memory, but MAGA is not our most urgent political problem. Long before Trump’s caustic presidencies corporate oligarchy took command of federal governance, tilting public policy routinely to favor corporate interests over the wellbeing of the nation. Senator Van Hollen knows this He rages against “...rigging the government in favor of billionaires and corporations while leaving the rest of us to pay the price.” (See his website .) Senator Schumer, on the other hand, is part of the problem. Over the years he has taken more than $19 million in campaign contributions from corporate sources, notably from the Wall Street banks. He is supported handsomely by AIPAC and other pro-Israel groups. Related: No Kings? SCOTUS Has Been a Workable Stand-In for 223 Years As an agent of corporate oligarchy Schumer is not the person to challenge it. We need Van Hollen. Tackling corporate oligarchy, regaining a functioning democracy, calls for his independent, bold, and determined effort. Democracy in America was sabotaged—corporate oligarchy germinated—about thirty years ago. Arandom convergence occurred, of several absurd Supreme Court decisions, Ronald Reagan’s misbegotten presidency, and two world-class hypocrites, Bill and Hillary Clinton. In the late 1800’s the Supreme Court declared U.S. corporations to be legal persons, with rights guaranteed by the Constitution, including the freedom of speech and the right “to petition government for a redress of grievances.” A century later the Court said spending money in political campaigns is a form of free speech and therefor could not be abridged. And lobbying could not be abridged, either: the right of petition guarantees that. Corporations were empowered to donate as much and lobby as much as they pleased, potentially to dominate the crafting of public policy. Only one brute fact prevented them from overcoming democracy altogether. Until late in the 20 th century. corporations were numerous, typically small, and in fierce competition with others. They simply could not afford to lavish money on office seekers, or to hire expensive lobbyists. Enter Ronald Reagan in 1981, whose presidency was guided not by the problems and opportunities facing the nation, but by his obsession with neoliberal ideology. Government is the problem, he said, stifling free enterprise with burdensome regulations. For most of the 20 th century, for example, American corporations had been stifled by anit-trust laws, preventing them from growing into the savage behemoths of the Gilded Age. That’s why they were small, competitive, and cash-strapped. Reagan suspended enforcement of those laws. Thus unstifled American corporations, through mergers and acquisitions, plummeted in number and exploded in size. Some 3,908 corporations are traded on the stock exchanges these days, almost exactly half the high-water mark of 8,090 in the last century. Most of them in fact pose no threat to democracy, but the largest of them do: the top 500 American corporations account for 91.2% of the total of U.S. market capitalization. Here we’ll find the corporate oligarchs. Reagan’s dogmatism drove virtually every industry in the country into textbook oligopoly—a few giant corporations in control, largely escaping the constraints of competitive pricing. Today ten gigantic combines of supermarket chains sell more than 90% of the all the groceries bought nationwide. This condition holds for nearly every other item of consumer goods, from books to power tools. Diminished competition inevitably raises prices; in the U.S. today, according to economist Thomas Phillipon, living costs for American families have escalated by about $5,000 per year. Ronald Reagan is responsible for the affordability crisis raging today, not Donald Trump. Trump merely exacerbates it. Related: The Peril of Spectacle, Especially Jeffrey Epstein’s Next came the Clintons. Over the course of their four presidential campaigns, Bill and Hillary Clinton claimed to be the champions of working class Americans. But during those years they accepted from Wall Street banks a total of $93 million . In exchange they destroyed the Democratic Party’s historic affiliation with American labor. It began in 1992. Bill Clinton, taking a cue from Republican candidates, enlisted corporate sources for much of his campaign funding. In office he rewarded his benefactors by moving the Democratic Party sharply rightward: “The era of big government is over,” he announced, and then took action to “...end welfare as we know it.” In Clinton’s preferred term the New Democratic Party joined the Republicans in accommodating, even welcoming corporate oligarchy. Chris Van Hollen at the time was serving in the Maryland legislature. He sponsored the Maryland Fair Campaign Finance Act, previewing his concern with the issue today. The next president George W. Bush embraced corporate oligarchy, taking us into a fraudulent "war on terrorism." In fact a war for oil and empire, the American people paid in blood and taxes while the nation’s corporations prospered. The grip of corporate oligarchy was tightening, and then in 2010 the Supreme Court decided Citizens United. The guard rails vanished. The millions in corporate campaign finance surged into the billions.Senator Van Hollen watched as the peril grew, and in 2019 he introduced a Constitutional amemdment to overturn Citizens. “It’s time we finally end the outside influence of special interest spending that is corrupting our democracy,” he said at the time. Corporate oligarchy prevailed. In the 2024 presidential campaign, small individual contributions ($200 or less) amounted to 16% of the total. That could be called the American people’s effort. “Business” donations, according to the Open Secrets organization, totaled 60.4%. And corporate lobbying? Corporations outspend citizen groups by a factor of 86:1. The American people are stratospherically outgunned. Democracy was defeated long before Trump’s autocracy: his Administration is merely corporate oligarchy on steroids. Defeating MAGA will strip away its steroids, but not corporate oligarchy’s hammerlock. Chris Van Hollen as Majority Leader will be a potent adversary. Note: this article was drawn from a book the author is completing, The Triumph of Corporate Oligarchy: How It Defeated Democracy, Ravaged a Thriving Nation, Normalized Fraudulent Warfare, and Brought Forth Donald Trump

articles.title: The Jungle (1906)
articles.author: Rochester Red Star: News from Rochester DSA
articles.content: by Upton Sinclair Upton Sinclair (1878 – 1968) was a socialist journalist and author, and unsuccessful Democratic candidate for governor of California in 1934 on the “End Poverty in California (EPIC) Platform.” The Jungle is best known for its unappetizing descriptions of the meat industry. As Sinclair lamented, “I aimed at the public’s heart, and by accident I hit it in the stomach.” But Sinclair’s work carries more explicitly anti-capitalist themes than commonly discussed. In the following excerpt, Lithuanian immigrant Jurgis reflects on his introduction to socialism by Polish immigrant Ostrinski, comparing the treatment of workers with that of hogs led to slaughter. – GLH Until long after midnight Jurgis sat lost in the conversation of his new acquaintance. It was a most wonderful experience to him – an almost supernatural experience. It was like encountering an inhabitant of the fourth dimension of space, a being who was free from all one’s own limitations. For four years, now, Jurgis had been wondering and blundering in the depths of a wilderness; and here, suddenly, a hand reached down and seized him, and lifted him out of it, and set him upon a mountain-top, from which he could survey it all – could see the paths from which he had wandered, the morasses into which he had stumbled, the hiding places of the beasts of prey that had fallen upon him. There were his Packingtown experiences, for instance – what was there about Packingtown that Ostrinski could not explain! To Jurgis the packers had been equivalent to fate; Ostrinski showed him that they were the Beef Trust. They were a gigantic combination of capital, which had crushed all opposition, and overthrown the laws of the land, and was preying upon the people. Jurgis recollected how, when he had first come to Packingtown, he had stood and watched the hog-killing, and thought how cruel and savage it was, and come away congratulating himself that he was not a hog; now his new acquaintance showed him that a hog was just what he had been – one of the packers’ hogs. What they wanted from a hog was all the profits that could be got out of him; and that was what they wanted from the workingman, and also that was what they wanted from the public. What the hog thought of it, and what he suffered, were not considered; and no more was it with labor, and no more with the purchaser of meat. That was true everywhere in the world, but it was especially true in Packingtown; there seemed to be something about the work of slaughtering that tended to ruthlessness and ferocity – it was literally the fact that in the methods of the packers a hundred human lives did not balance a penny of profit. When Jurgis had made himself familiar with the Socialist literature, as he would very quickly, he would get glimpses of the Beef Trust from all sorts of aspects, and he would find it everywhere the same; it was the incarnation of blind and insensate Greed. It was a monster devouring with a thousand mouths, trampling with a thousand hoofs; it was the Great Butcher – it was the spirit of Capitalism made flesh. Upon the ocean of commerce it sailed as a pirate ship; it had hoisted the black flag and declared war upon civilization. Bribery and corruption were its everyday methods. In Chicago the city government was simply one of its branch offices; it stole billions of gallons of city water openly, it dictated to the courts the sentences of disorderly strikers, it forbade the mayor to enforce the building laws against it. In the national capital it had power to prevent inspection of its product, and to falsify government reports; it violated the rebate laws, and when an investigation was threatened it burned its books and sent its criminal agents out of the country. In the commercial world it was a Juggernaut car; it wiped out thousands of businesses every year, it drove men to madness and suicide. It had forced the price of cattle so low as to destroy the stock-raising industry, an occupation upon which whole states existed; it had ruined thousands of butchers who had refused to handle its products. It divided the country into districts, and fixed the price of meat in all of them; and it owned all the refrigerator cars, and levied an enormous tribute upon all poultry and eggs and fruit and vegetables. With the millions of dollars a week that poured in upon it, it was reaching out for the control of other interests, railroads and trolley lines, gas and electric light franchises – it already owned the leather and the grain business of the country. The people were tremendously stirred up over its encroachments, but nobody had any remedy to suggest; it was the task of Socialists to teach and organize them, and prepare them for the time when they were to seize the huge machine called the Beef Trust, and use it to produce food for human beings and not to heap up fortunes for a band of pirates. It was long after midnight when Jurgis lay down upon the floor of Ostrinski’s kitchen; and yet it was an hour before he could get to sleep, for the glory of that joyful vision of the people of Packingtown marching in and taking possession of the Union Stockyards! articles.title: Progressives Must Rethink Race
articles.author: Tom Hall
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. It’s time for Americans, including progressives, to try new thinking about race. The right-wing e-newsletter The Dispatch called the midterms “A Blowout.” The Donald’s immediate response was to double down on the politics of division and to appoint extreme racist Stephen Miller as his chief of staff for the remainder of his term. Much of the “progressive” response to the midterms has been a mixture of gloating, recriminations about the “Democratic Party Machine,” and announced plans for retribution—against both enemies and natural allies. At the October 2–4 Left Coast Forum in Los Angeles, a conservatively dressed, gray-haired gentleman with a complexion darker than Herschel Walker’s sat in the back row of several sessions. He didn’t speak most of the time, but when he did, he was soft-spoken and not confrontational. When I approached him, he identified himself as an MSW and a social policy analyst. One issue came to the fore each time I spoke to him or heard him speak during a session. He asserted that “race” is a false construct and that focusing on it risks distracting us from the real problems and issues facing society. Science has pretty well eliminated any objective basis for racial classifications. Even before European mercantilism and colonialism initiated global mass trading that mixed heretofore separate population groups and civilizations, people were people. We share essentially 100% identical DNA, regardless of individual variations in gene expression affecting eye color, skin pigmentation, perceived “beauty,” handedness, disease susceptibility, and a million other characteristics. Related: What If AI Learns That Inequality—not Humanity—is the Problem? People descended from other primates that lived in groups. And people, from their earliest manifestations, have been group-focused primates. As small groups merged into villages, then cities and states, they retained their group identities and practiced behaviors that pitted groups against other groups, both for survival and for gain. This pattern is not unique to evil Caucasian colonists trying to subjugate Africans, Asians, Latin Americans, and Native Americans. It is what history and science tell us about humans on every continent, humans of every color, and humans of every political persuasion, going back as far as archaeological remains reveal evidence of group living, group warfare, and individual violence. “Race” as a social definition is much more recent and is essentially an economic rather than a scientific or social reality. As early as 1640, a Virginia colonial court sentenced a Black man to lifetime servitude while sentencing his White co-defendants to only extended indenture. And in 1661, Virginia started crafting laws to officially recognize “race-based” slavery. These were decisions of economic policy, not scientific reality. American slavery was novel. Spain instituted slavery across the Caribbean, first trying to coerce Native Americans into providing labor as part of purported religious instruction and conversion. But Native Americans had the home-court advantage and easily disappeared into forests and jungles when they didn’t want to be slaves. Following Christopher Columbus’s example of seizing people from lands he explored, traders traveling to Africa seized Africans and brought them to the New World. The Africans didn’t have the Native Americans’ local knowledge or connections to local tribes that might have enabled them to escape bondage. And the traders had many customers eager for captive workers who had no opportunities for escape. So the 1661 Virginia slavery legislation was a formalization of an emerging economic system that used an artificial and unscientific basis for providing legal economic benefits to plantation owners. Then, a 1662 Virginia law held that “Black” children’s status followed that of their mother rather than their father. Therefore, a child born to an enslaved mother was automatically a slave, even if the child’s father was a free “White” man. By breeding their slaves, plantation owners could increase their wealth without economic investment. Monopoly capitalism at its finest. Related: Trump, Iran and the New Middle East Power Shift As European societies increasingly recognized that human slavery was entirely inconsistent with Christianity, and as Latin American colonies threw off French and Spanish colonial rule (Haiti in 1804 and Mexico in 1821), the United States doubled down on human slavery. The plantation economy of the American South was the greatest source of income for the new nation. And it depended entirely on slave labor. Although sermons and treatises defended human slavery as beneficial and “Christian,” more and more voices were raised in support of abolition. Slave owners and the governments that depended on slavery-generated income passed laws making it illegal to teach slaves to read, write, and do arithmetic. Enslaved Christian preachers were criminalized, with increasingly severe restrictions imposed after preachers like Nat Turner encouraged freedom in the name of Christianity. Leading up to the American Civil War, there was no longer any pretense. Race-based human slavery was an economic engine. In 1845, Southern plantation owners who were members of the Baptist Church in America broke away from the main Baptist organization and founded the Southern Baptist Convention (SBC). The two groups’ theology remained the same, with the exception that the SBC proclaimed that “Black” people were created inferior by God and were destined to exist in eternal servitude to the White master race. The creation of the SBC was an entirely economic move, with no pretense of any scientific basis. It was simply an announcement by wealthy plantation owners that their economic interests mandated the creation of their own new religion, rejecting the Christian teachings of both Catholic and Protestant churches around the world. The same logic underlay the creation of the Klan and all Jim Crow laws. But the economic interests were not specific to race. The successes of the labor movement in the first decades of the 20th century were limited by efforts to convince White workers to see “Black” and “Latin” workers as economic enemies. The interest was not racial separation but dissension between visibly identifiable groups of workers, keeping them from forming stronger unions that might demand bigger pieces of the industrial pie. Historians of the late 18th and early 19th centuries point to identical efforts by American diplomats negotiating with Native American tribes. While numerous diplomats recorded Native American efforts to persuade tribes to put aside their differences and consolidate their efforts to resist land takeovers in the Ohio Valley and other areas southeast of the Mississippi River, the record of treaties made and then broken consistently shows diplomats’ efforts to deal with individual tribes rather than groups (unions?) of tribes. After World War II, which followed the great economic democratizing successes of the New Deal, the Civil Rights Movement gained momentum. While many of today’s “progressives” and “revolutionaries” spout stock “Marxist” phraseology against religion, the Civil Rights Movement did what labor unions had failed to do. Churches of various denominations encouraged the involvement of all people in the struggle. Fundamentalists who believed that Catholics sided with Satan and that Jews killed Jesus agreed to work with Catholics and Jews to end segregation. Looking at innumerable civil rights activities, we focus on a few heroic women, such as Rosa Parks and Mamie Till-Mobley. The movement was built on the labor of women before there was a Women’s Movement. It was built on the work of nuns, the efforts of women working in Jewish congregations and Protestant churches, women performers spreading messages of freedom, and the work of women who, decades earlier, had developed tactics and messages for women’s suffrage. Related: From Bull Connor to ICE: The Return of State-Sanctioned Violence The Women’s Movement met as much resistance as the Labor Movement had, albeit with less overt violence, from the same forces that, in the 1930s, 1950s, and the 1960s, had opposed every other effort to get working people to see themselves first as working people with common interests, rather than as people with different skin tones, national and religious backgrounds, or differently formed eyelids. In a rejection, even a denial, of science, firefighters and police officers were encouraged to resist the inclusion of women in their “male” professions. And the same foolishness continues today as the nation’s secretary of defense rails that women can’t perform in leadership roles or in combat, even as every modern nation around the world has successfully integrated women into its war machine. The same secretary, for the same divide-and-conquer reasons, is denying qualified “Black” and “Brown” men promotions and positions of authority. It’s easy to see why corporations that thrive on low-paid labor and those that suck down tax dollars for unproven weaponry want to promote divisive thinking. Billions of dollars are at stake in every budget year. No one wants to give money to workers instead of allocating it to management bonuses and shareholder dividends. But it is our tax money. It is our consumer money. Discrimination against Asians, Blacks, Latinos, and Native Americans has never been about race. It has been about economic advantages. Cheap Chinese and Irish laborers were both imported to build our railroads. Both were called “inferior,” while the corporations that imported them really meant “cheaper.” There were times when Eastern Europeans and Southern Europeans were imported as cheaper and supposedly “inferior” workers. Hungarians and other Eastern Europeans (collectively disparaged as “Hunkies”) filled steel mills. Italians (“Wops”) filled cheap factory and agricultural jobs. The use of derogatory nicknames helped—and continues to help—maintain their categorization as separate from and inferior to “real Americans.” In the 1640 Virginia case involving John Punch, racial distinctions that had no meaning for the defendants were beneficial to businessmen. Three men, all indentured to Hugh Glyn, ran away from Virginia but were captured in Maryland. They were punished for fleeing from indentured servitude. John Punch was a “Black” servant. The two runaways with him were “White.” The two White runaways were sentenced to longer periods of indenture. John Punch was sentenced to lifetime servitude. Racism is not a natural phenomenon. Running away from slavery was a regular feature of life in the American colonies. And although Africans generally had darker skin tones than Native Americans, runaway slaves were often accepted and adopted into Native American clans and families. Related: Privatize the Profits, Socialize the Costs But racism can be learned. As colonial intrusion shrank Native American communities, those communities tried to find ways to resist, fight back, and reclaim lands taken from them by settlers moving west from the growing United States. The Cherokee Nation tried to model its government on that of the United States, developing its own written language, writing a constitution, and forming a bicameral legislature and a judiciary independent of executive functions. The Cherokees had prospered economically. They built plantations and exported cotton and other crops to the United States. They worked their plantations with slave labor, even while incorporating free “Black” people into Cherokee families and communities. But when the Cherokee Constitution was adopted in 1827, it explicitly disenfranchised “Black” people, including the “Black”-fathered children of Cherokee women. To succeed in business relations with their dominant neighbor, Cherokees learned to adopt American racism after having been welcoming to “Black” people fleeing slavery for more than two centuries. Similarly, both French and Spanish legal systems recognized property ownership and legal personhood for women. Women could buy, inherit, manage, and sell their own property. But when the United States took over French and Spanish territories, it imposed English “common law,” under which a woman’s property became her husband’s and her legal personhood was subsumed into his. There were no biological or other scientific reasons for this. It was simply a feudal system that concentrated financial control in limited hands. The experiences of indentured servants, Native Americans abandoning traditional societal inclusiveness, workers trying to organize, and women trying to live in their respective societies each teach us that scientific realities can be overcome by social training. The Labor Movement, Civil Rights Movement, Women’s Rights Movement, and Gay Rights Movement all teach us that training can move societies away from artificial bigotries. The forces of economic self-interest will always push divisiveness. It is in their interest to increase conflict and pit their workers and customers against each other. The fear of losing a job opportunity to another applicant is similar to the fear of losing the last Cabbage Patch doll to another customer in the holiday rush. Pushing fear as a marketing technique to increase profit is natural. It is as old as competing preachers proclaiming that they each have access to the only eternal truths. But let us not solely blame businessmen and the defenders of social “traditions.” As the October Left Coast Forum also showed us, “leftist” organizations have their own traditions of divisive thinking. Marxists point out the dogmatic purity of Leninists, who disdain backsliders and people who differ over points of dogma. And “everybody” hates the Trotskyites. It is easy to find “progressives” who are eager to attack their allies over details of policies on which they nominally agree. “Race” is one of those policies. For many progressives, accepting the traditional, conservative definition that racial distinctions exist is their natural starting point. After all, they have learned all their lives that race exists and that race matters. They “know” that it’s real because they’ve experienced its effects all their lives. Changing that thinking will not stop those who benefit from racism from continuing to practice it, continuing to promote it, and continuing to benefit from it. But changing the training can, has, and will disrupt the efforts of bigots and profiteers and move society toward further abandoning the artifices created by colonial businessmen in the early 17th century. The Cherokee National Constitution of 1827 didn’t prevent the forced military removal of the Cherokee Nation from its land under Andrew Jackson. But years later, the Cherokee removed the explicitly racist, exclusionary language. If those whom our Founding Fathers called “the savage Indians” could learn to adopt and then abandon artificial constructs, shouldn’t we “superior” modern people be able to learn at least as well? Related: AI, the Bible, and the Battle Over Who Controls Knowledge President Obama delivered a speech on his racial position and got himself elected president of the United States. He delivered the long-overdue beginnings of a national healthcare program, which led to his condemnation by both racist, pro-business healthcare backers and “progressives” who thought he didn’t deliver enough, despite the strident and staunch opposition embodied in Mitch McConnell’s “one-term president” decree. The 16th Amendment moved the needle. It didn’t make our tax system fair, just fairer. The 19th Amendment gave women the vote. It didn’t make all women vote sensibly, any more than male suffrage makes MAGA men vote sensibly. The failure of the Equal Rights Amendment did not stop the development of the Women’s Movement or the great (if still inadequate) strides toward equality for women. The same can and must be said of race. Race is an artificial construct, created and maintained for the benefit of economically controlling interests. It has no objective reality. But it enjoys widespread belief and acceptance. A proper progressive response to racial discrimination in our society is not to continue to accept it as “reality” but rather to begin to attack the fake construct itself and work to rob it of its social acceptance. Exploiting racial themes for fundraising and political leverage is effective. We have increasingly diverse representation at all levels of government. People seeking government services encounter government employees from an increasingly broad range of ethnicities, religions, and national origins, all to the benefit of society. Exposing pernicious racism when it presents itself remains a necessary part of the process. It leads to progress. We need to find new language for talking about “race”—new language that is not grounded in acceptance of conservative and business-centered divisiveness, definitions, and terminology. New language that can speak both to progressives and to those who are coming to see that their support for the Donald and for corporate oligarchy was misplaced and self-injuring. It won’t be easy, but new language can help us develop a new construct about “race,” a new understanding that it isn’t real. Working out new language will be messy, as all important social progress is. We learned in the early 20th century to “dial” our telephones. How many of today’s children “dial” their cell phones without any idea of what the term even means? What verb will emerge to refer to the process of mechanical arms reaching out to catch descending rocket ships, replacing the long sentence used by SpaceX to describe its new process of handling returning spaceships? Race itself was once a new term. François Bernier, a French physician, proposed dividing humans into four races back in 1684, 44 years after John Punch was sentenced to lifetime servitude. Ignoring the fact that it took some years for Dr. Bernier’s idea to spread widely, 342 years is long enough for his faulty concept to be abandoned. But it should take many, many fewer years to convince Americans to abandon it, as so much of the rest of civilization has. Related: Young Blood Isn’t Enough—and Neither Is Experience The midterm elections were a wake-up call, showing that American voters are frustrated and open to change. But open to what change? Republicans, with their embrace of the Donald’s appointment of Stephen Miller and their defense of Pete Hegseth, have shown their intractability. What of progressives? Can they rethink their commitment to conservative, economically driven definitions of race? Can they meet the voters’ challenge to change old, stale, economically devastating definitions and assumptions? Can they learn to abandon false but profitable language for a new construct—a world that denies the false construct?

articles.title: US suspends military cooperation with Ecuador amid human rights violations probe
articles.author: BreakThrough News
articles.content: The US government announced a move that has surprised many in Ecuador. For several weeks, Washington and Quito have been touting, through press releases, various military and intelligence operations against organized crime in Ecuador. According to several media outlets , including The Atlantic and The New York Times , the US has decided to suspend these joint operations until it clarifies incidents in which abuses and killings may have been committed against suspects in custody of Ecuadorian forces on September 23 . According to US media reports , Washington wants to determine whether Carlos Muñoz, alias “Charlie” – one of the leaders of Los Choneros, one of Ecuador’s most prominent criminal gangs – along with other suspects, was killed while in custody. On September 23, Ecuador’s Minister of Defense, Gian Carlo Loffredo, released images showing a man believed to be alias “Charlie” and other dead bodies lying in a bloody mess alongside weapons in a pickup truck. In a post on X, Loffredo says : “Alias ‘Charlie’ belonged to the Los Choneros and Frente Oliver Sinisterra groups in Colombia, had ties to Mexico’s Jalisco New Generation Cartel, and his main mission was to sow terror in our country.” Read more: ‘They laughed at what they had done’: Ecuadorian fishermen sue US after surviving drone strike at sea In addition, Loffredo added : “The Ecuadorian Armed Forces, in cooperation with US Southern Command within the framework of the Internal Armed Conflict, have eliminated one of the highest-value military targets on Ecuadorian soil… We promised: ‘Prison or hell,’ and this one didn’t make it to prison.” The alleged investigation is also seeking to determine whether US military personnel participated in the operation. However, the Times clarified that the US Department of Defense issued a statement saying that no US soldier participated in the alleged crimes and that the Trump administration “[takes] allegations of misconduct by our partners seriously.” This incident comes just one week after Pete Hegseth visited Quito and held a meeting with Ecuador’s president, the right-wing Daniel Noboa, who is currently in the midst of a local election campaign. A few days ago, several Ecuadorian fishermen filed a complaint against the Trump administration for allegedly bombing their boat on the high seas and detaining them before sending them against their will to El Salvador. Two fishermen were injured in the attack. A major setback for the Noboa administration Despite repeated promises, Noboa’s government has failed to halt the worst wave of violence in the country’s history, which has so far claimed thousands of lives. Instead, it found a boost to its security policy – based on a quasi-perpetual state of emergency – in US military and logistical support. The news comes just days before local elections in which Ecuador will elect 24 prefects, 221 mayors, and hundreds of council members and local government board members. Noboa has led the election campaign in support of his party’s candidates. He has not yet commented on Washington’s decision. Read more: With the main opposition party suspended, Ecuador returns to the polls In light of the serious allegations, Loffredo said that cooperation has not completely ended: “We continue to work together to combat criminal structures.” He added that there are people who would like to see the recent military cooperation between Washington and Quito fall apart: “They want to damage these relationships that have yielded positive results, but we have a job to do, and the talks went very well.” The Trump administration has found in right-wing governments such as Noboa’s allies that support its foreign policy and reinforce its geopolitical project to reaffirm US hegemony over the West, a project embodied in the Shield of the Americas. The agreement signed by the vast majority of South American nations provides for the conduct of various military operations between the US military and the armed forces of each country to, as the agreement states, combat drug trafficking and terrorism anywhere on the American continent. For now, it is unclear what Washington’s decision will be if the allegations implicating Ecuadorian authorities in extrajudicial killings are proven true. What is certain is that the decision came at a politically inopportune time for Noboa, and it remains to be seen whether it will have significant immediate electoral consequences.

articles.title: A Tribute to Blacklisted Lyricist Yip Harburg: The Man Who Put the Rainbow in The Wizard of Oz
articles.content: This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form. AMY GOODMAN : Today, we pay tribute to Yip Harburg. His name may not be familiar to many, but his songs are sung by millions around the world, like jazz singer Abbey Lincoln. ABBEY LINCOLN : Bing Crosby sang it, Ike Quebec played it, and Yip Harburg wrote it. [singing] Once I built a railroad, made it run Made it race against time Once I built a rairoad, now it’s done Brother, can you spare a dime? AMY GOODMAN : And Tom Waits. TOM WAITS : [singing] Once I built a tower way up to the sun With bricks and mortar and lime. AMY GOODMAN : Judy Collins, and Dr. John from New Orleans, Peter Yarrow. AL JOLSON : [singing] Say, don’t you remember, Don’t you remember they called me Al It was Al, Al all the time. AMY GOODMAN : That’s Al Jolson. And our beloved Odetta. ODETTA : [singing] Don’t you remember, I’m your pal Say, brother, can you spare a dime? Buddy, can you spare a dime? AMY GOODMAN : “Brother, Can You Spare a Dime?” may well be a new anthem for many Americans. The lyrics to that classic American song were written by Yip Harburg. He was blacklisted during the McCarthy era. During his career as a lyricist, Yip Harburg used his words to express antiracist, pro-worker messages. He’s best known for writing the lyrics to The Wizard of Oz , but he also had two hits on Broadway: Bloomer Girls , about the women’s suffrage movement, and Finian’s Rainbow , a kind of immigrants’ anthem about race and class and so much else. Today, in this Democracy Now! special, we pay tribute to Yip Harburg’s life. Ernie Harburg is Yip’s son and biographer. He co-wrote the book Who Put the Rainbow in The Wizard of Oz?: Yip Harburg, Lyricist . I met up with Ernie Harburg at the New York Public Library for Performing Arts at Lincoln Center years ago when they are exhibiting Yip Harburg’s work. Ernie Harburg took me on a tour. ERNIE HARBURG : The first place is business about words, and one of them is that the songs, when they were written back in those days, anyhow, always had a lyricist and a composer, and neither one of them wrote the song. They both wrote the song. However, in the English language, you know, you have “This is Gershwin’s song,” or “This is” — they usually say the composer’s song. I’ve rarely ever heard somebody say, “This is Yip Harburg’s song” or “Ira Gershwin’s song.” Both of them would be wrong. The fact is, two people write a song. So I’m going to talk about Yip’s lyrics and then lyrics in the song. Now the first thing we’re looking at here is an expression really of Yip’s philosophy and background, which he brings to writing lyrics for the songs. And what it says here is that songs have always been man’s anodyne against tyranny and terror. The artist is on the side of humanity from the time that he was born a hundred years ago in the dire depths of poverty that only the Lower East Side in Manhattan could have when the Russian Jews, about 2 million of them, got up out of the Russian shtetls and ghettos, and the courageous ones came over here and settled in that area, what we now know as the East Village. And Yip knew poverty deeply, and he quoted Bernard Shaw as saying that the chill of poverty never leaves your bones. And it was the basis of Yip’s understanding of life as struggle. AMY GOODMAN : Let’s go back to how Yip got his start. ERNIE HARBURG : Yip was, at a very early age, interested in poetry, and he used to go to the Tompkins Square Library to read, and the librarians just fed him these things. And he got hooked on every one of the English poets, and especially O. Henry, the ending. He always has a little great ending on the end of each of his songs. And he got hooked on W.S. Gilbert, The Bab Ballads . And then, when he went to Townsend High School, they had them sitting in the seats by alphabetical order, so Yip was “H” and Gershwin was “G”, so Ira sat next to Yip. One day, Yip walked in with The Bab Ballads , and Ira, who was very shy and hardly spoke with anybody, just suddenly lit up and said, “Do you like those?” And they got into a conversation, and Ira then said, “Do you know there’s music to that?” And Yip said, “No.” He said, “Well, come on home.” So they went to Ira’s home, which was on 2nd Avenue and 5th Street which is sort of upper from Yip’s poverty at 11th and C. And they had a Victrola, which is like having, you know, huge instruments today, and played him H.M.S. Pinafore . Well, Yip was just absolutely flabbergasted, knocked out. And that did it. I mean, for the both of them, because Ira was intensely interested that thing, too. That began their lifelong friendship. Then Ira went on to be one of the pioneers, with 25 other guys, Jewish Russian immigrants, who developed the American Musical Theater. And it was only after — in 1924, I think, that Ira’s first show with George Gershwin, his brother, that they started writing together. AMY GOODMAN : The Gershwins’ Porgy and Bess in 1940. ERNIE HARBURG : Yip’s career took a kind of detour, because when the war, World War I, came and Yip was a socialist and did not believe in the war, he took a boat down to Uruguay for three years. I mean, he refused to fight in the thing. That’s shades of 1968 and the Vietnam War, right? AMY GOODMAN : And why didn’t he believe in World War I? ERNIE HARBURG : Because he was a full, deep-dyed socialist who did not believe that capitalism was the answer to the human community and that indeed it was the destruction of the human spirit. And he would not fight its wars. And at that time, the socialists and the lefties, as they were called, Bolsheviks and everything else, were against the war. And so, when he came back, he got married, he had two kids, and he went into the electrical appliance business, and all the time hanging out with Ira and George and Howard Dietz and Buddy De Sylva and writing light verse for the F.P.A Conning Tower. And the newspapers used to carry light verse, every newspaper. There were about 25 of them at that time, not two or three now owned by two people in the world, you know. And they actually carried light verse. Well, Yip and Ira and Dorothy Parker, the whole crowd, had light verse in there, and, you know, they loved it. So, when the crash came and Yip’s business went under, and he was about anywhere from $50,000 to $70,000 in debt, his partner went bankrupt. He didn’t. He repaid the loans for the next 20 or 15 years, at least. Ira and he agreed that he should start writing lyrics. AMY GOODMAN : Let’s talk about what Yip is most known for: Finian’s Rainbow , The Wizard of Oz . Right here, what do we have in front of us? ERNIE HARBURG : We have a lead sheet. We are in the gallery of the Lincoln Center for the Performing Arts, and there’s an exhibition called “The Necessity of Rainbows,” which is the work of Yip Harburg. And we are looking at the lead sheet of “Brother, Can You Spare a Dime?” which came from a revue called Americana , which — it was the first revue, which was — had a political theme to it: at that time, the notion of the forgotten man. You have to remember what the Great Depression was all about. It’s hard to imagine that now. But when Roosevelt said, “One-third of the nation are ill-clothed, ill-housed and ill-fed,” that’s exactly what it was. There was at least 30% unemployment at those times. And among Blacks and minorities, it was 50, 60%. And there were breadlines and — Now, the rich, you know, kept living their lifestyle, but Broadway was reduced to about 12 musicals a year from prior, in the '20s, about 50 a year, OK? So it became harder. But the Great Depression was deep down a fact of life in everybody's mind. And all the songs were censored — I use that loosely — by the music publishers. They only wanted love songs or escape songs, so that in 1929 you had “Happy Days Are Here Again,” and you had all of these kinds of songs. There wasn’t one song that addressed the Depression, in which we were all living. And this show, the Americana show, Yip was asked to write a song or get the lyrics up for a song which addressed itself to the breadlines, OK? And so, he, at that time, was working very closely with Jay Gorney. Jay had a tune, which he had brought over with him when he was 8 years old from Russia, and it was in a minor key, which is a whole different key. Most popular songs are in major. And it was a Russian lullaby, and it was da, da, da, da, da, da, da, da, da. And Jay had — somebody else had lyrics for it: “Once I knew a big blonde, and she had big blue eyes. She was big blue” — like that. And it was a torch song, of which we talked about. And Yip said, “Well, could we throw the words out, and I’ll take the tune?” All right. And if you look at Yip’s notes, which are in the book that I mentioned, you’ll see he started out writing a very satiric comedic song. At that time, Rockefeller, the ancient one, was going around giving out dimes to people, and he had a — Yip had a satiric thing about “Can I share my dime with you?” You know? But then, right in the middle, other images started coming out in his writings, and you had a man in a mill, and the whole thing turned into the song that we know it now, which is here and which I can read to you. And if you do this song, you have to do the verse, because that’s where a lot of the action is. AMY GOODMAN : Can you sing it to me? ERNIE HARBURG : All right, I’ll try. It won’t be as good as Bing Crosby or Tom Waits. [singing] They used to tell me I was building a dream, And so I followed the mob, When there was earth to plow Or guns to bear, I was always there Right on the job. They used to tell me I was building a dream, With peace and glory ahead, Why should I be standing in line, Just waiting for bread? YIP HARBURG : [singing] Once I built a railroad I made it run, Made it race against time. Once I built a railroad; Now it’s done. Buddy, can you spare a dime? AMY GOODMAN : Yip Harburg singing in 1975. YIP HARBURG : [singing] Once I built a tower To the sun, Brick and rivet and lime; Once I built that tower; Now it’s done. Brother, can you spare a dime? AMY GOODMAN : When was this song first played? ERNIE HARBURG : In 1932. And in the Americana revue, every critic, everybody took it up, and it swept the nation. In fact, paradoxically, I think Roosevelt and the Democratic Party really wanted to tone it down and keep it off the radio, because playing havoc with trying to not talk about the Depression, which everybody did. You remember the Hoover thing, not only “Happy Days Are Here Again,” but “Two Chickens in Every Pot,” and so forth. Nobody wanted to sing about the Depression either, you know. AMY GOODMAN : Yet, Yip Harburg was a supporter of FDR . ERNIE HARBURG : Yes. But politics are politics, you know, and the thing was that, in fact, historically, this was, I would say, the only song that addressed itself seriously to the Great Depression, the condition of our lives, which nobody wanted to talk about and nobody wanted to sing about. AMY GOODMAN : Ernie Harburg, son of Yip Harburg. When we come back from our break, we’ll talk about The Wizard of Oz , Finian’s Rainbow and other shows. [break] AMY GOODMAN : This is Democracy Now! , democracynow.org, The War and Peace Report . I’m Amy Goodman, as we continue with our Democracy Now! special, on our journey through Yip Harburg’s life with his son, Ernie Harburg. Ernie talks about how Yip Harburg wrote the lyrics to The Wizard of Oz . ERNIE HARBURG : Actually, Yip did more than the lyrics. When they were — when Yip and Harold Arlen were called in to do the score of The Wizard of Oz , it was Yip who had this executive experience in his electrical appliance business and also had become a show doctor, so he was — that is, when a show wasn’t working, you would call somebody and try to fix it up. He had an overview of shows and he had an executive talent. And so, he was always what they called a “muscle man” in a show, all right? And he’d already worked with Bert Lahr in a great song, “The Woodchopper’s Song,” and — AMY GOODMAN : Wait a second. Bert Lahr, the lion? ERNIE HARBURG : The lion. Bert Lahr and most of these people were from vaudeville and burlesque. And Yip knew them in the ’20s, but he actually worked with Bert Lahr in this light — Walk a Little Faster and another revue. I forget that name, but he and — Yip and Arlen gave Bert songs to sing, which allowed him to satirize the opera world, if you want, or a send-off of rich, you know. And so, they had that relationship. Also, Yip knew Jack Haley, the tin woodman. And Yip also worked with Bobby Connolly as a choreographer in the early '30s on his shows, who was also the choreographer for The Wizard of Oz . So he had a cast here with Arlen who were, you know, sort of Yip's men. You know what I mean? So, when Yip went to Arthur Freed, the producer, who was too busy to work on this musical, and Mervin LeRoy had nothing to do with it, practically, because he had never done a musical before, so it became a vacuum in which the lyricist entered, because he was all ready to do so. Yip was always an active, you know, organizer. And so, the first thing he suggested was that they integrate the music with the story, which at that time in Hollywood they usually didn’t do. They’d stop the story, and you’d sing a song. They’d stop the story and sing a song. That you integrate this — Arthur Freed accepted the idea immediately. Yip then wrote — Yip and Harold then wrote the songs for the 45 minutes within a 110-minute film. The munchkin sequence and into the Emerald City and on their way to the wicked witch, when all the songs stopped, because they wouldn’t let them do anymore. OK? You’ll notice then the chase begins, you see, in the movie. AMY GOODMAN : Why wouldn’t they let them do anymore? ERNIE HARBURG : Because they didn’t understand what he was doing, and they wanted a chase in there. So, anyhow, Yip also wrote all the dialogue in that time and the setup to the songs, and he also wrote the part where they give out the heart, the brains and the nerve, because he was the final script editor. And there was eleven screenwriters on that. And he pulled the whole thing together, wrote his own lines and gave the thing a coherence and a unity, which made it a work of art. But he doesn’t get credit for that. He gets “lyrics by E.Y. Harburg,” you see? But, nevertheless, he put his influence on the thing. AMY GOODMAN : Who wrote The Wizard of Oz originally, the story? ERNIE HARBURG : Yeah, Frank L. Baum was an interesting kind of maverick guy, who at one point in his life was an editor of a paper in South Dakota. And this was at the time of the populist revolutions or revolts, or whatever you want to call it, in the Midwest, because the railroads and the Eastern city banks absolutely dominated the life of the farmers, and they couldn’t get away from the debts that were accumulated from these. And Baum set out consciously to create an American fable so that the American kids didn’t have to read those German Grimm fairy stories, where they chopped off hands and things like that. You know, he didn’t like that. He wanted an American fable. But it had this underlay of political symbolism to it that the farmer — the scarecrow was the farmer. He thought he was dumb, but he really wasn’t; he had a brain. And the tin woodman was the result — was the laborer in the factories. With one accident after another, he was totally reduced to a tin man with no heart, all right, on an assembly line. And the cowardly lion was William Jennings Bryan, who kept trying — was a big politician at that time, promising to make the world over with the gold standard, you know? And the wizard, who was a humbug type, was the Wall Street finances, and the wicked witch was probably the railroads, but I’m not sure. All right? So it was a beautiful match-up here with Frank Baum and Yip Harburg, OK, because in the book, the word “rainbow” was never once mentioned. And you can go back and look at it. I did three times. The word “rainbow” is never once mentioned in the book. And the book opens up with Dorothy on a black-and-white world, that Kansas had no color. Just read the first paragraph in it. So, when they got to the part where they had to get the song for the little girl, they hadn’t written it yet. They had written everything else. They hadn’t written the song for Judy Garland, who was a discovery by one of Yip’s collaborators, Burton Lane. And nobody knew the wonder in her voice at that time. So they worked on this song, and at that time, Ira, Yip, Larry Hart and the others thought that the composer should create the music first. Now, they were both locked into — the lyricist and the composer were locked into the storyline and the character and the plot development. So they both knew that at this point there was a little girl in trouble on the Kansas City environment, all right, and that she yearned to get out of trouble, all right? So Yip gave Harold what they call a “dummy title.” It’s not the final title, but it’s something that more or less zeroes in on what the situation is all about and what — this little girl is going to take a journey, all right? So Yip gave him a title: “I Want to Get on the Other Side of the Rainbow.” YIP HARBURG : Now, here’s what happened, and I want you to play this symphonically! OK, I said, “My god, Harold! This is a 12-year-old girl wanting to be somewhere over the rainbow. It isn’t Nelson Eddy!” And I got frightened, and I said, “I don’t — let’s save it. Let’s save it for something else. But don’t — let’s not have it in.” Well, he felt — he was crestfallen, as he should be. And I said, “Let’s try again.” Well, he tried for another week, tried all kinds of things, but he kept coming back to it, as he should have. And he came back, and I was worried about it, and I called Ira Gershwin over, my friend. Ira said to him, he said, “Can you play it a little more in a pop style?” And I played it, with rhythm. OK, I said, “Oh, well, that’s great. That’s fine.” I said, “Now we have to get a title for it.” I didn’t know what the title was going to be. And when he had [sings] dee-da-dee-da-da-da-da, [talking] I finally came to the thing, the way our logic lies in it, “I want to be somewhere on the other side of the rainbow.” And I began trying to fit it: “On the other side of the rainbow.” When he had a front phrase like daa-da-da-da-da — now, if you say “eee,” you couldn’t sing “eee-ee.” You had to sing “ooooh.” That’s the only thing that would get a — and I had to get something with “oh” in it, see: “Over the rain” — now, that sings beautifully, see. So the sound forced me into the word “over,” which was much better than “on the other side.” JUDY GARLAND : [singing] Somewhere over the rainbow Way up high, There’s a land that I heard of Once in a lullaby. ERNIE HARBURG : Anyhow, Yip — Arlen worked on it. He came up with this incredible music, which, if anybody wants to try it, just play the chords alone, not the melody, and you will hear Pachelbel, and you will hear religious hymns, and you will hear fairy tales and lullabies, just in the chords. No one ever listens to that, but try it, if you play the piano. And at any rate, on top of these chords, then Harold started the thing off with an octave jump: “Somewhere” — OK, and Yip had no idea what to do with that octave jump. Incidentally, Harold did this in Paper Moon , too, if you remember. Let’s see how did that start? YIP HARBURG : [singing] It’s only a paper moon Sailing over a cardboard sea But it wouldn’t be make-believe If you believed in me ERNIE HARBURG : And Harold was a great composer. So Yip wrestled with it for about three weeks, and finally he came up with the word. You see, this is what a lyricist does: the word, to hit the storyline, the character, the music. It’s an incredible thing. “Some-where.” All right, and then when you put in an octave, you get “some-where,” OK, and you jump up, and you’re ready to take that journey. All right? Where? “O-ver the rainbow.” OK? And then you’re off! It’s not a love song. It’s a story of a little girl that wants to get out. She’s in trouble, and she wants to get somewhere. Well, the rainbow was the only color that she’d see in Kansas. She wants to get over the rainbow. But then, Yip put in something which makes it a Yip song. He said, “And the dreams you dare to dream really do come true.” You see? And that word “dare” lands on the note, and it’s a perfect thing, and it’s been generating courage for people for years afterwards, you know? JUDY GARLAND : [singing] Somewhere over the rainbow Skies are blue, And the dreams that you dare to dream Really do come true. ERNIE HARBURG : That’s the way that the whole score came. AMY GOODMAN : Was it a hit right away? ERNIE HARBURG : No, it wasn’t. This was supposed to be an answer, MGM’s answer to Snow White and the Seven Dwarves , and of about 10 major critics at that time when The Wizard of Oz came out, I would say only two liked the show. The other eight said it was corny, that it was heavy, that Judy Garland was no good, and so forth. Oh, yeah. You could read again in the book, Who Put the Rainbow on The Wizard of Oz? , by Harold Meyerson and Ernie Harburg. But it persisted, you know? And then, in 1956, when television first started saturating the nation — AMY GOODMAN : More than 20 years later. ERNIE HARBURG : More than 20 years later. I don’t think they even had their money back from the show, see? MGM sold the film rights to CBS , who then put it on. And it hit the top of the — it broke out every single record there was, and it’s been playing every year since then. ERNIE HARBURG : No — well, yes! The winkies were good people, and they were played up there. If you go back and read the book, you will see that they were a lovely, decent kind of people, yes. All these lines from the film have entered the American language in a way that people don’t even know where they came from. AMY GOODMAN : How did Yip feel in the late 1950s, when it was a hit, when people started hearing it all over the world? ERNIE HARBURG : Well, I think they were quite surprised, along with the film moguls, you know, and the fact that — years and years later, he and Harold both said that they did not know what depth and strength that that song “Over the Rainbow” had. And also, one other one, the song “Ding! Dong! The Witch Is Dead” is a universal liberation, a freedom, a cry for freedom, you know, which isn’t seen like that, but it — one time, when some tyrannical owner of an airlines company stepped down, all the employees started singing “Ding! Dong! The Witch Is Dead.” So people use these words. And during the war, World War II, “We’re Off to See the Wizard” was sung by troops marching, you know? But nobody knows that Yip wrote the words, you see. Now, Harold wrote the music, and the songs were Yip and Harold. That’s it.
